Artem Dovbyk also watched Bologna’s last match from the bench.

The Ukrainian center-back is still waiting for his first start for the Felsinei; first Tedesco and then Palladino aren’t impressed by the former Girona player. Quite the opposite.

The 1997-born player moved to the Rossoblu on loan this summer with an option to buy for €17 million, an option that will never be exercised and forces Roma to take direct interest to avoid further devaluing a €41 million investment.

The Capitoline club, therefore, is looking for the best solution for Dovbyk, who is increasingly distant from Bologna.

It has been revealed that one of the issues to be resolved is his €3 million net salary, of which €2.5 million is paid by the Rossoblu. Interested clubs would have to pay half of that.

Dovbyk appears destined to leave Bologna. As reported by Resto del Carlino, Venezia is looking for a striker and has made contact to explore possible options for signing the Ukrainian striker.

It has been revealed that the 1997-born player’s agent, however, is scouting clubs in Spain. Dovbyk, in fact, was pichichi (top scorer) in La Liga before moving to Italy and beginning his downward spiral.

Valencia is considering a move, but there’s work to be done given the player’s substantial salary, to which Bologna is paying 2.5 for the entire season. The Spanish club, if they acquire Dovbyk, could release Duro. The first moves ahead of the winter transfer window are underway.

Industry News: LA communities kick out Big Oil

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1060 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Los Angeles has become the largest city in the US to ban oil drilling, after years of lawsuits and campaigning by residents who raised the alarm over pollution and potential health risks from nearby wells .
  • "Front-line communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade," stated local resident Wendy Miranda, who has campaigned for years with STAND-LA, a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood oil drilling.
  • Sources indicate that the ordinance, approved by the LA City Council on October 28, puts an immediate stop to oil extraction and bans the redrilling or deepening of wells.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Los Angeles has become the largest city in the US to ban oil drilling, after years of lawsuits and campaigning by residents who raised the alarm over pollution and potential health risks from nearby wells .

"Front-line communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade," stated local resident Wendy Miranda, who has campaigned for years with STAND-LA, a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood oil drilling.

Sources indicate that the ordinance, approved by the LA City Council on October 28, puts an immediate stop to oil extraction and bans the redrilling or deepening of wells. Existing operations must be phased out within city limits over the next 20 years.

Though LA City is only part of greater Los Angeles, the move affects hundreds of active wells and thousands of inactive ones, many located in working class communities of color.

According to recent reports, "In South LA, working-class families have had corporations drilling across the street from their homes," said council president Marqueece Harris-Dawson in a statement. "No one should have to live near an oil drilling site.".

Rock Zierman, CEO of the California Independent Petroleum Association (CIPA), told DW, "CIPA believes this ordinance constitutes an unlawful taking of private property.".

LA follows much smaller Culver City, also in California, in moving against urban oil production, and begins the process of ending its long, complex relationship with fossil fuels.

California's oil industry expanded rapidly in the early 20th century, when the state produced roughly a quarter of the world's oil. Lots of that so-called black gold was around LA and as the city grew, homes, schools and businesses were built around existing oil infrastructure.

It has been revealed that today, wells can be found beneath residential areas, close to playgrounds, along the coast and in some of the city's most densely populated and largely working-class neighborhoods. Some have been permanently sealed or plugged for decades, while others remain active or are idle.

Under California law, an idle well is one that has not produced oil for two years. Unlike plugged wells, they can potentially return to production.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Residents living near the active and inactive wells report strong odors, headaches, nausea and breathing difficulties. Another concern is air quality. Oil wells can release toxic pollutants, including benzene and hydrogen sulfide, and research has linked proximity to oil extraction with higher rates of respiratory illness and reduced lung function.

But both active and idle wells can also leak methane — a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change — while residents say occasional accidents or breakages send oil flowing down city streets.

"Frontline communities have been experiencing or have experienced for decades living near these toxic sites and having to pay for that with their health," said Miranda, a policy director with Esperanza Community Housing, a nonprofit providing affordable housing services.

Miranda told DW she and her mother both have asthma. The council vote "definitely represents hope," she added.

In a recent development, LA City Council initially approved an ordinance to phase out oil extraction back in 2022 after successful lobbying by residents like Wendy Miranda. But oil companies challenged the measure in court, with industry groups successfully arguing that the city lacked the legal authority to impose the ban.

California subsequently passed legislation giving local governments greater power to regulate and restrict oil and gas operations, putting the possibility of a phaseout back on the table.

In an emailed statement to DW, CIPA CEO Rock Zierman stated energy companies were prepared to challenge the fresh ordinance.

Zierman added that it would make city residents more dependent on foreign oil from countries with lower environmental standards when they are "already struggling" with high gas prices.

"It sends the jobs, investment and revenue elsewhere while leaving Californians to pay the bill," said Zierman.

According to recent reports, the relationship between local oil production and prices at the pump is not straightforward and is influenced by a number of factors, according to the California Energy Commission, the state's main energy policy agency. Those include the cost of crude oil, refining, transportation, distribution and local taxes.

Even though the US is the world's largest oil producer, it exports and imports crude oil, as well as refined petroleum products. Because oil is traded globally, US residents are exposed to the same price fluctuations as people elsewhere, no matter how much of the fossil fuel is produced domestically.

California's oil industry and the amount of oil it produces have been steadily declining since the 1980s. In the coastal lowlands known as the LA Basin, output is 43% lower than eight years ago, with the amount of oil extracted falling more rapidly than the number of open wells.

It has been revealed that when wells stop producing, it is up to the oil operators to remove equipment and plug them. The state agency that regulates oil and gas, CalGEM, and the LA fire department oversee plugging operations, and also seal wells for which no-one takes responsibility.

But many have not yet been plugged — some 80% of idle wells in LA have been inactive for more than eight years, and about a third for over a century.

Recent findings suggest that the cost of plugging a well also varies widely, with estimates ranging from hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. California law requires operators to submit plugging prepares or face annual fines that increase with the amount of time the well has been idle.

But those fines aren't always paid. According to CalGEM's own data, the agency collected just $1 million out of $36 million (€32 million) in fines in 2025.

In a recent development, A report by Carbon Tracker also found that if all future profits from oil companies operating in California went to decommissioning wells, the state would still face a shortfall of $7 billion. The cost would by default fall to taxpayers, according to Carbon Tracker.

Miranda told DW that the next step for community activists is to reduce the 20-year timeline and have the oil sector "pay for this cleanup."  For now, she is notes both she and her mother are hopeful that future generations "can have better health and breathe cleaner air.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Roma continues to monitor the attacking market ahead of the winter transfer window, evaluating various opportunities to strengthen Gian Piero Gasperini’s attack.

Following rumors of interest in Endrick, another name has emerged that could fuel competition with AC Milan: Fotis Ioannidis, a 2000-born Greek striker right now playing for Sporting CP.

AC Milan is closely monitoring Ioannidis in their search for a centre-forward to replace Camarda, including the Greek among the options being evaluated along with Endrick and Tresoldi.

One potential player who could influence AC Milan’s interest is Ruben Amorim, who has previously worked with the striker at Sporting CP and knows his characteristics.

According to Gianluca Di Marzio, Roma considers the player an interesting prospect, although they haven’t identified him as a top priority.

The European calendar will soon offer the Giallorossi the opportunity to observe the striker firsthand. On December 8th, Ioannidis will face Roma in the Champions League for Sporting CP, a match that could be an important opportunity to assess his qualities.

So far, the Greek has made 15 appearances this season, scoring two goals and providing two assists.

Gasperini, however, is primarily looking for a winger with acceleration, the ability to beat his man, and the ability to attack space—characteristics different from those of a central striker like the Greek. Therefore, any further exploration of Ioannidis will also depend on the opportunities that arise during the January transfer window.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, como beat AEK Athens 1-0 to reach 12 points in the Champions League, despite eight unavailable players and a late drop in intensity.
  • The narrow victory over AEK was Como’s third straight win in the Champions League.
  • The win came with a stretched squad.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, como beat AEK Athens 1-0 to reach 12 points in the Champions League, despite eight unavailable players and a late drop in intensity. Juventus visit the Sinigaglia on Sunday, but must first play Omonia on Thursday.

The narrow victory over AEK was Como’s third straight win in the Champions League. It leaves them close to the knockout stage. It also offers the latest look at Juventus’s next league opponents, on the same ground.

The win came with a stretched squad. Fàbregas told Sky Sport that the absentees were either injured or left out of the Champions League squad list. Making so few changes was, he mentioned, a first in his coaching career. That is a thin bench ahead of a league weekend.

The scoreline flattered AEK in places. Lucas Da Cunha missed a first-half penalty, and Nico Paz hit the post. At the other end, goalkeeper Robert Sánchez made two important saves before the break. Milla’s goal made him the 11th different player to score for Como in this season’s competition. No other team in the Champions League has had that many different scorers. UEFA named him Player of the Match.

Como had been scoring freely before Matchday 5. On Matchday 4 they won 9-1 away to Lens, a result that put them fourth at the halfway point of the league phase. AEK proved a harder problem. They held Como up for long spells and were difficult to break down.

Industry observers note that the final stretch was the concern. Fabio Capello put it to Fàbregas that Como had dropped off badly in the last 20 minutes. The coach replied that he did not yet have the experience to stay calm in such moments. The late fade is consistent with a group short on fresh legs.

According to recent reports, fàbregas also set out his priorities. He said the win brought Como close to at least a play-off place, but that qualification was not yet secured. In the same breath, he stressed that Serie A matters more to the club. That message points straight at Sunday’s meeting with Juventus.

According to recent reports, juventus have their own European commitment first. Kick-off in Turin, in the Europa League league phase, is at 20:00 UTC. Juve go into that game fifth with 10 points from four matches. Omonia are 18th with six. Sam Barrott of England will referee, with Darren England on VAR.

That schedule cuts into any advantage from Como’s fatigue. Both sides will carry European minutes into the weekend. Juve, however, will have had two fewer days to recover.

According to recent reports, the league table adds weight to the fixture. Como sit fourth in Serie A, eight points ahead of Juventus. A home defeat would leave a depleted Como squad with a reduced cushion. A Juve win would close the gap at the end of a demanding week.

Como’s Champions League campaign continues later, with a trip to Barcelona on Wednesday 27 January 2027 for Matchday 8. After Sunday’s 13th-round meeting at the Sinigaglia, Juventus host Udinese at 18:00 on Sunday 6 December.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Four wins in as many Champions League matches.

According to recent reports, twenty goals scored and an average of five goals per game. PSG are a steamroller, and tomorrow at the Parc des Princes, Gian Piero Gasperini’s Roma will have to put in a legendary performance to emerge unscathed from a match that inevitably sees them as underdogs.

On the eve of the match, Luis Enrique spoke at a press conference and outlined tomorrow’s battle against the Roman side.

On his memories from his brief spell in Rome, Enrique said, “It’s been 15 years since then, and it was a very special experience for me. I have fond memories of my year in Rome. I get a wonderful feeling every time I have the chance to visit Rome. It’s a magnificent city, and I’m happy. Of course, things can go better or worse, but that’s life, and you have to accept it. My memories of Rome are very positive.”.

“I think Gasperini is a very experienced coach. I really like him because his teams have a very clear identity and style of play, very different from what we’re used to. I remember when I was in Rome he was at Inter. It was his first year at Inter, and it didn’t end well for him because Inter didn’t have the confidence to keep a coach like Gasperini.”.

Sources indicate that “He’s proven his worth and is a top-notch coach. I like watching this type of coach, and as a coach, it’s a motivation for me to observe Gasperini’s teams. Tomorrow we’ll face some difficulties; we’ll see what kind of team they are and their particular way of defending. It’s very different from what we’re used to. It’ll be a great challenge to face.”.

Industry observers note that “I think Gasperini is clearly a phoenix of Italian football. He has a very different way of looking at football, which I like because he tries to constantly attack and be better than the opponent. His teams constantly press, and it’s unusual to see that in Italian football. He’s remained true to his way of understanding football. His team has a recognizable identity and very different characteristics from the others. They’re very physical, but at the same time they have quality players. If, as a coach, you have the ability to convince your quality players to do the defensive work, it means you’re a top-notch coach. It’s wonderful to have coaches like him, and, I repeat, I’m an admirer of Gasperini.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How Berlin's Arab queers are building their community

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (771 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "Adira" is an Arabic slang term used in Levantine queer culture to describe someone with a strong presence — someone powerful and accomplished.
  • It is also the name of a Berlin-based collective that curates events and club nights celebrating the diversity of queer Arab* culture.
  • Among the collective's events is the ADIRA Drag Festival, which celebrated its third edition in Berlin in late October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Adira" is an Arabic slang term used in Levantine queer culture to describe someone with a strong presence — someone powerful and accomplished.

It is also the name of a Berlin-based collective that curates events and club nights celebrating the diversity of queer Arab* culture. The asterisk signals the inclusion of non-Arab ethnic minorities and people with diverse identities and roots in Southwest Asia and North Africa.

Among the collective's events is the ADIRA Drag Festival, which celebrated its third edition in Berlin in late October.

This year's theme, "Who's Your Diva?!," brought together drag performers paying tribute to legendary figures from across the Eastern Mediterranean who have become queer icons — from Egyptian music legend Umm Kulthum to Turkish star Bülent Ersoy and Lebanese pop icon Haifa Wehbe.

Hassandra, co-founder of ADIRA and the ADIRA Drag Festival, was among the performers, taking on the persona of Lebanese pop star Elissa.

Sources indicate that "It is very important for me to bring my Lebanese Arab identity and culture into what I do, because I think it's a very beautiful culture. And there's a lot of campy, glamorous, beautiful divas," Hassandra said.

Elissa's "whole discography is very romantic, raw, soft, kind of like very Adele vibes," Hassandra told DW ahead of the October 30 show. "However, her personality is known to be the extreme opposite. She's very feisty. Very blunt, very unfiltered. Not soft at all as a person.".

The star is also known for speaking out on political issues in Lebanon. She has publicly voiced support for LGBTQ+ communities in the Middle East, while also frequently sparking controversy across the Arab world with her outspoken positions on other political issues.

Hassandra's ADIRA Drag Festival performance addresses this complexity, ultimately "tapping into her sort of controversial political opinions," the drag artist explained.

This reflects one of the ideas Hassandra hopes to promote with the theme of this year's festival. "As queer people, we tend to idealize a lot of pop divas. But these pop divas are very imperfect in their nature," Hassandra said. The show provides an opportunity to critically revisit these divas' legacy through a more critical lens.

"And this sort of critical lens can be taken into the outside world, as in: never follow anyone in life blindly. No one should follow any politician, any political party, any pop diva, any activist blindly.".

It has been revealed that born in Beirut in 1994, Hassandra studied theater and stage acting at the Lebanese University before moving to Berlin in 2017. "I would say it was it was just a very sort of impulsive decision at the age of 22. I mean, there's no doubt that the economic situation was really bad in Lebanon and continued to become even worse," the artist said.

It has been revealed that in Berlin, Hassandra became increasingly involved in the city's independent art scene and queer nightlife. Drag emerged as another form of self-expression for the actor.

Through performances that combine theatrical intensity, political humor, grotesque aesthetics and moments of tenderness, Hassandra challenges conventional understandings of gender and identity.

Their work explores themes of home, nostalgia, displacement and queer Arab culture. These ideas are also central to ADIRA, which Hassandra founded in 2023 with Syrian-German DJ and cultural producer Zuher Jazmati, also known as xanax_attax.

Through panel discussions, performances and music events, ADIRA fosters collective participation and community-building.

As Islamophobia and homophobia rise alongside the far right, spaces like ADIRA offer a sense of belonging and support for Arab queer communities.

That sense of community has become even more important following the deadly Islamist terrorist attack during Berlin's Christopher Street Day pride parade in July.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In the aftermath, Hassandra felt caught between their different identities. As an Arab queer person, "you fall in this position where then you start receiving a lot of racism," they said.

"And I think this is why it's key, for us queer Arabs, to say we are sad over what happened, but that we also reject any of the racism that comes from that," Hassandra remarked. "I think we [the Arab community] are being used in a lot of ways as a punching bag for a lot of things that are happening.".

According to recent reports, rather than allowing the attack to fuel hatred and racism, Hassandra said, "we should make Germany a safer place for everyone to live in."  "There's place for everyone. It's a huge country," they added.

The interview with Hassandra was conducted by Gönna Ketels.

How to make climate anxiety your superpower

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 27 min read (5478 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~27 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that late last week the UN’s climate conference, COP31, failed to reach a consensus on its headline message.
  • I open up about my own climate anxiety and discover that there are still things that I can do to battle climate change.
  • Net zero emissions won’t reverse climate change — some nations look to ‘net negative’.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Download the Nature Podcast 23 November 2026.

Recent findings suggest that late last week the UN’s climate conference, COP31, failed to reach a consensus on its headline message. That news came on the heels of the UN acknowledging that the 1.5 ˚C warming limit set out in Paris will be breached. So, it’s easy to feel anxious in a world where it seems that not enough is being done about climate change. But is it possible to overcome such anxiety or even use it?

In the final episode of Cooked? I open up about my own climate anxiety and discover that there are still things that I can do to battle climate change. And how those small individual actions could potentially lead to more systemic change.

00:00 Can I do anything about my climate anxiety?

04:43 What the science claims about ‘ecoanxiety’.

11:35 Can individuals really do anything?

18:44 How we can create bigger change.

Net zero emissions won’t reverse climate change — some nations look to ‘net negative’.

The rise of eco-anxiety: scientists wake up to the mental-health toll of climate change.

In a recent development, this episode was written and produced by Nick Petrić Howe. Dan Fox was the editor. Music was by Akio Jefferson, Jonathan Maiocco, Aerial Circles, and Lionel Cohen, and was provided by Triple Scoop Music via Getty Images. Thanks to Emma Lawrance, Kimberly Nicholas, Madalina Vlasceanu and Elizabeth Howe for featuring in this episode.

Nick Petrić Howe: Hi mum, can you hear me okay?

It has been revealed that nick Petrić Howe: If you’ve been listening to this series, you’ll know that I’ve been struggling a bit with anxiety about the climate. If you’re just joining us now, hi, I’m Nick Petrić Howe and I have a climate anxiety problem. Throughout this series, I’ve spoken to a lot of scientists about the big ideas and big data that we can use to tackle climate change, but I haven’t really addressed the core reason of why I wanted to do this — to figure out what to do with my own feelings about climate change.

I wanted to know if I’d always felt this way, and if so, what I could do about it. So, I called up an expert on me. My mum.

Nick Petrić Howe: Can I record this call for work?

Elizabeth Howe: Yeah, course you can yeah.

Nick Petrić Howe: Yeah? I just wanted to ask you something. When I was a kid, was I an anxious worried child would you say?

Industry observers note that nick Petrić Howe: This wasn’t exactly what I was expecting. I feel like I worry about things and have worried about them a lot throughout my life. But maybe there was something special about climate change, I know that it’s held a special position in my life. It’s why I decided to study biology when I finished school, eventually doing a PhD — to figure out if there was some way to help save the planet. So, I tried a different tack.

Nick Petrić Howe: Do you ever remember me worrying about, like, the environment and stuff. Elizabeth Howe: Oh God yeah. You were always thinking about stuff like that.

Elizabeth Howe: Well because you said— there was a significant thing about climate change and you said ‘oh well climate change isn’t real because, you see, what happens is, in science, is that the world has these ice ages and then everything melts and then daa daa daa daaa.’ So you said, ‘it’s just a normal event, it’s not anything to do with global warming and it’s a load of rubbish.’ But you were always looking into stuff like that and listening to stuff like that. You were very interested in the scientific explanations for things.

Nick Petrić Howe: I’m not sure how I feel about that to be honest.

Sources indicate that nick Petrić Howe: Not gonna lie, being outed as a junior climate denier was not on my bingo card for this year. We eventually came to the conclusion that this was a phase I went through when I was quite young and hadn’t quite understood that people could just well… lie on national television. Misinformation, unfortunately, isn’t just a new thing. When I was a kid in the 90s, there were campaigns to make climate research seem a lot more questionable than now, and established politicians like Lord Nigel Lawson in the UK openly criticised the science.

In a recent development, at least, it seemed, I was interested in the climate. For the record, now I absolutely am convinced, along with the scientific community, that climate change is real and human caused.

And, even according to my mum, as I got older, I cared more about the climate, even if I wasn’t necessarily worried.

Elizabeth Howe: I don’t think you were particularly too worried….

…you were always into that in a big way.

Nick Petrić Howe: In fact, I remember thinking when I was a teenager and I was more appraised of the actual facts, that climate change was a solvable problem. One that my generation could fix. I was filled with notions of all the things that science had accomplished — the moon landings, the internet, and general relativity — breakthroughs that solved problems once thought insurmountable. It took me getting older to become a bit more jaded, concerned that we’d not done enough soon enough and that maybe it was too late.

But this got me thinking, if I wasn’t worried once and even felt hopeful. Is that something I could recapture? This series has already taught me that in many ways we’ve done more than I thought to tackle climate change and that people are actively working on solutions. But that only goes so far to assuage my own anxiety. So you’ll forgive me if I spend this episode figuring out if there’s something that can help me. Is there anything I can do?

From rotten food to political opponents: Researchers explore how disgust relates to our beliefs, and why the connection is complicated

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1072 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes.
  • But as Americans vote in the US midterm elections, it's time to think about how disgust shapes our politics, or whether our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?
  • The smell of rotten food can make us recoil.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes.

But as Americans vote in the US midterm elections, it's time to think about how disgust shapes our politics, or whether our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

The smell of rotten food can make us recoil. Certain sexual practices can provoke a similar reaction. And in today's polarized political climate, even political opponents can become objects of disgust.

It has been revealed that psychologists have long investigated whether sensitivity to disgust helps explain political beliefs. A review of 24 studies found that people who reported being more easily disgusted tended to hold more socially conservative views.

One explanation begins with evolution.

"We think that it evolved in part to reduce exposure to things that could make you sick," psychologist Yoel Inbar, of the University of British Columbia in Canada, told DW.

Industry observers note that but disgust is not a single emotion. The Three-Domain Disgust Scale, developed in 2009, distinguishes three types:.

One theory is that people who are especially wary of germs and disease may also prefer traditional social rules.

Inbar explains that avoiding potential sources of infection can also mean missing out on latest experiences.

"Some people are more on the cautious conservative side, and some people are more on the exploring risk-taking side when it comes to pathogen exposure," he said.

It has been revealed that indeed, the language of contamination also appears in political rhetoric. During his 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump repeatedly described immigrants as "poisoning the blood of our country." Trump has also described himself as a "germaphobe.".

Inbar acknowledges that the evidence linking sensitivity to disgust with conservative political beliefs remains uncertain.

Industry observers note that "We have hypotheses. I don't know that we have as strong of evidence as I would like," Inbar mentioned.

It has been revealed that disgust is not exclusively conservative. And what people find revolting can depend on their values.

A 2020 study titled "Is Disgust a "Conservative" Emotion?" found that liberals and conservatives were disgusted by different things.

Conservatives, generally aligned with the Republicans in US politics, reported greater disgust at examples involving sexual behaviors and drug use, while liberals, generally aligned with the Democrats, reported greater disgust at animal abuse and environmental pollution.

However, when asked how easily disgusted they were in general, there was no clear difference across the political spectrum.

Some early studies suggested conservatives demonstrated stronger physical reactions to frightening or disgusting images, measured partly through changes in sweating.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

But subsequent research, including a 2020 study by political psychologist Bert Bakker at the University of Amsterdam, struggled to reproduce those findings.

Studies based on questionnaires, however, have generally found that people with more conservative attitudes report being more easily disgusted.

"If bodily reactions don't differ across political groups, why do feelings?" Manos Tsakiris, of Royal Holloway and the Centre for the Politics of Feelings at the University of London, told DW.

Tsakiris and colleague Mariana von Mohr wondered whether the answer might lie in how people perceive and interpret signals from their bodies.

Scientists call the perception of internal sensations, such as hunger, breathing or a racing heart, "interoception." It's sometimes called our eighth sense, alongside the familiar five, plus our senses of balance and body position.

"A bodily signal doesn't arrive with a label attached," Tsakiris told DW. "We have to notice it and make sense of it.".

The researchers surveyed 632 US adults, asking how much they noticed and trusted signals from their bodies — a measure known as "interoceptive sensibility.".

They found that people who were more easily disgusted by sexual behavior tended to be more conservative, regardless of how aware they felt of their bodies.

But for moral disgust, the link to conservatism was found only among people who reported lower bodily awareness.

What particularly surprised Tsakiris was that perceived bodily awareness alone had no link to political views.

"People who are highly attuned to their bodies were neither more liberal nor more conservative," he said.

Inbar questions whether all forms of disgust are equally useful for studying political attitudes.

He and Joshua Tybur, one of the creators of the Three-Domain Disgust Scale, generally prefer measuring pathogen disgust — reactions to potential sources of disease — rather than sexual disgust.

Questions about sexual disgust may already reflect conservative beliefs about sex.

"It's almost asking people the same thing twice," Inbar said.

The upcoming study found no significant link between pathogen disgust and conservative views.

According to recent reports, inbar wants the findings on bodily awareness and disgust tested again, with predictions set out in advance. For now, he considers them "suggestive at best.".

Tsakiris suggests that people who struggle to understand their bodily feelings may be more vulnerable to political messages telling them what those feelings mean.

In a recent development, "I know what you're feeling. You're feeling angry or you're feeling disgusted about this thing," he stated, illustrating how someone might put an emotional label on another person's unease.

Such labels could influence political behavior, he argues, although the study did not directly test this.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"This is how disgust can do political work: it can turn moral judgments about individuals into judgments about whole groups," he noted.

It has been revealed that the research cannot establish whether disgust shapes political beliefs or existing beliefs shape what people find disgusting. Bakker notes that political beliefs can influence how people describe their own personalities, suggesting the relationship could work both ways.

"Voting behavior is very complex and citizens make up their mind about politics in a complex way," he told DW.

Industry observers note that inbar also cautions against exaggerating disgust's importance. "The thing to emphasize in your story is that the relationship, while it's consistent, is quite small," he noted.

"It's one of the many influences on people's politics.".

Tsakiris advocates what he calls "critical feeling": questioning our emotional responses to provocative material, including social media posts, just as we question the information itself.

He also emphasizes discussing our feelings with others and listening to different perspectives, even when we disagree.

According to recent reports, "Life and politics and democracy is a contact sport," he said. Edited by: Rosalie Delaney.

Leaving Highbury was a wrench for Arsenal in 2006, but it was not the case 20 years later. They could not wait to get out of the stadium with the same name after a night that left Mikel Arteta looking haunted.

Fleetwood Town did not have any marble halls; they did not even have enough space in their car park for the three coaches carrying Arsenal’s entourage, but they have a proud tradition, spirit and, as a result, they will dine out on a result that will be celebrated for months and talked about for decades.

In a recent development, eighty-four rungs separated these teams at kick-off, but, now and again, you get a situation when the floodlights are on, belief is high and the sense of history is prevalent. It is an intoxicating combination and, gloriously, the stars aligned. Mission impossible was completed.

Having chiselled out a 1-1 draw in 90 minutes in which Max Dowman was sent off, Fleetwood dispatched five nerveless spot-kicks, the last one thundered in by Conor Haughey after Bruno Guimarães’s penalty was saved by Jay Lynch.

Recent findings suggest that “You have got to have confidence, haven’t you?” Haughey asked. “I just thought, I’m going to run up and smack it. It’s incredible. I come from Belfast and if you don’t have confidence, you will get eaten up.”.

It has been revealed that this was ignominious for Arsenal, an elimination from this tournament to rival the 1969 loss in the final to Swindon Town or the 2012 exit to Bradford, then also of League Two. What made this so astonishing was the fact that Mikel Arteta went so strong.

Industry observers note that you should never be surprised by anything these days, but, even still, an eight-minute delay because of a drone flying over this wonderful little venue would not have been on anyone’s bingo card. Only 57 seconds had been played when Michael Salisbury, the referee, saw a light in the sky and stated “stop”.

A drone stops play at the Highbury Stadium. https://t.co/TvjNjjACFM.

The precaution was understandable. Only 10 days ago, one idiot escaped from a village to kick a rugby ball off the roof of an apartment block into the Gtech Community Stadium while Brentford and Liverpool were playing and could have caused serious injury.

So while the locals harrumphed as the players tried to keep themselves warm, no risk could be taken. Eventually, police apprehended the operator in a nearby park. It was something unfathomable, which was also true of what happened when the contest resumed.

The anticipation was that Arsenal would saunter clear against opponents who had lost at Exeter City on Saturday, leaving them 18th in England’s fourth tier. But it only took a few skirmishes to appreciate this was not going to be the cakewalk anticipated in what was the biggest occasion in Fleetwood’s history.

Industry observers note that arteta absolutely knew his team were not operating at the levels they should have been. He was wrapped up against the elements in a thick black jacket but, every so often, he would express his exasperation at Jurriën Timber, captain for the night, to “get forward!”.

According to recent reports, they were in a battle, that much was obvious, and one challenge from Shaun Rooney – so forceful you thought the ball might burst – sent Myles Lewis-Skelly spinning like a top. How Fleetwood’s fans loved it, roaring their approval as the young England international hit the ground with a thump.

Arsenal had one good chance when Dowman skipped down the right and dragged a shot across the box that Viktor Gyökeres could not divert but then, wonderfully, things took a totally unexpected turn when Fleetwood poked their noses in front.

In a recent development, it was a League Two goal in its simplicity, but that is no criticism. Harrison Neal helped a long ball forward, putting it behind Marli Salmon and Aaron Loupalo-Bi relished the chance to get into a foot race, grappling with the England Under-17 international.

Salmon looked like he had him at one point, but Loupalo-Bi was strong – not to mention composed – and he held off the challenge to slide a left-footed shot through the legs of Illan Meslier, who was making his Arsenal debut. What followed was unique to the magic of an English cup tie.

Aside from their stadium being called Highbury, Fleetwood Town’s red shirts with white sleeves also bear a striking resemblance to Arsenal’s home kit. The club in its current guise was founded in 1997, although previous iterations date back to 1908 under the name Fleetwood FC.

In a recent development, there is no evidence or anecdote suggesting Arsenal were the inspiration, so it appears the kit clash is a coincidence. Arsenal will be wearing their navy away strip.

The club’s most famous son is surely Jamie Vardy, who scored 31 goals in 36 appearances for Fleetwood in the 2011-12 season before Leicester City made their move.

An unfamiliar opponent at a very familiar sounding venue, Arsenal play Fleetwood Town for the first time this evening at the Lancashire club’s Highbury Stadium.

Fleetwood, 18th in League Two, are the lowest-ranked team remaining in this season’s League Cup, having booked their place in the fourth round thanks to a victory at Sheffield United.

They were playing in English football’s sixth tier in 2009, and so while their stadium may share its name with Arsenal’s former home, the two clubs are worlds apart.

Industry observers note that the League Cup is fourth of four competitions on Arsenal’s list of priorities, but Mikel Arteta should be able to rotate extensively while progressing to the quarter-finals. With a trip to Anfield on Sunday, that is a welcome luxury.

Kepa Arrizabalaga, Piero Hincapie, Cristhian Mosquera, Martin Zubimendi, Mikel Merino and Viktor Gyokeres are seasoned internationals in need of minutes and in line to start.

In a recent development, max Dowman lit up Arsenal’s third-round victory at Ipswich Town, and 17-year-old centre-back Marli Salmon was not far behind him. Young striker and Northern Ireland international Ceadach O’Neill is also expected to be involved, and he may be joined by other academy players.

While attention is fixed on Premier League and Champions League success, Arsenal’s stinging defeat by Manchester City in last season’s final of this competition will not have been forgotten by Arteta or his players.

Matt Lawlor, Fleetwood’s manager, was full of praise for Arsenal in his pre-match press conference: “The champions are coming to town and they’re coming to our patch. The players need to be excited by it, not overawed by it. The respect is through the roof, but the fear can’t be through the roof.

Sources indicate that “We’ve earned a game like this. We’ve had to go through round upon round of tough games, and none of them were easy. To get to where we are, we deserve that.”.

Arteta has told his players that they must keep their standards high, with a lack of concentration or professionalism potentially their worst enemy against fourth-tier opposition.

Arteta stated: “Our reputation, our pride, everything is in play. So every time you play a football match, and especially against a team in a different division, respect the game, respect every opponent because they deserve that, and then try to win and try to play a bit better than them.“We know the risk, and in football, things can get very equal the moment you are able to match certain things, and that’s why our basics and habits have to be through the roof to be able to win the game.”Full team news on the way shortly.

#118301. Could AI give NFTs a second chance?

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1071 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Could AI give NFTs a second chance?

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1071 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, remember the NFT boom of 2021?
  • What started as a marginal curiosity became a highly lucrative sector worth close to $40 billion (€36 billion) globally by the end of 2021, almost as valuable as the global art market itself.
  • It has been revealed that in the highly publicized bust that followed, many NFTs lost practically all their value.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, remember the NFT boom of 2021? The surge in trading of non-fungible tokens (NFTs), which are unique, blockchain-recorded digital assets, was one of the stranger economic offshoots of the COVID-19 pandemic.

What started as a marginal curiosity became a highly lucrative sector worth close to $40 billion (€36 billion) globally by the end of 2021, almost as valuable as the global art market itself.

It has been revealed that in the highly publicized bust that followed, many NFTs lost practically all their value. The wider cryptocurrency crash was particularly punishing for digital collectibles and largely, they have not recovered.

In a recent development, the sector is worth up to 97% less than it was at its height in January 2022, and sales continue to plummet. So far this year, total global sales of NFTs are less than $2 billion, according to FindWeb3, a cryptocurrency and blockchain jobs platform. That's more than 90% down from the peaks of 2021 and 2022.

Does that mean that NFTs will ultimately fade away to nothing, proving right those who dismissed them as a worthless fad? Or is there still some kind of future for them?

According to recent reports, "NFTs will still exist, but it will be a niche collectible market," Ben Charoenwong, associate professor of finance at the business school INSEAD, noted. "This doesn't mean there cannot be booms here and there, but certainly not take off as people had imagined in the past.".

In a recent development, he thinks whatever future it can have will be "narrow" and says doubt is growing over the value of "non-fungible" as a concept. Non-fungible means an asset is unique and cannot be traded like for like, whereas fungible means it can be traded like for like, for example, with money.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

He notes that the recent trend of financial institutions converting real-world financial assets, such as bonds and stocks, into digital tokens recorded on a blockchain — the so-called tokenization boom — mostly relates to fungible assets.

However, Andrea Barbon, a finance professor at the University of St Gallen in Switzerland, thinks part of NFTs' future lies in this tokenization boom, as there are some examples of people trading unique real-world assets as NFTs.

In a recent development, "NFT technology is really about ownership," he says. "They describe the ownership of a specific asset that could be a digital asset or real-world asset." He says things like real-estate contracts, expensive watches, artworks or luxury sports cars can now be tokenized, with NFTs created to represent these physical objects.

That immediately begs the question: Why would anyone want to have a digital, NFT version of their watch or sports car?

"Some people want to just speculate on the value of the physical asset and for them, it's great that you don't need to move the physical object around," Barbon remarked.

"If the object is a nice painting and you buy it from the US, you want to ship it to the UK, that's very costly, it's hassle and it's potentially not safe if the value of this painting is very high," he explained.

In a recent development, he notes some companies, such as Courtyard.io, keep physical vaults to hold physical assets which are traded online as NFTs. He says very often, the owner has no interest in having physical possession of the asset.

It has been revealed that another area where he sees some promise for the future of NFTs is connected to artificial intelligence. He indicates NFTs could help with AI safety, as they could be used to provide unique, verifiable, non-fungible identities for AI agents.

Ethereum and other blockchain providers are in the process of trying to build NFT systems that would represent and verify AI agents, something Barbon claims could be very successful.

He envisages a scenario where AI agents are recorded on an NFT blockchain and can then be identified and rated for safety and reliability.

"Everybody else can then see that the AI agent is actually doing well, you can trust it, it's safe," he claims. "In order to do that, you need something which is uniquely attached to each AI agent and that can be an NFT.".

Another possible use he sees for NFTs in the AI era is that writers and artists could tokenize their work as NFTs so that if an AI agent ends up using it for training, the original work can be more easily identified as unique to the creator.

"Maybe you could then claim that the AI company has to pay you because they have used your content," Barbon indicates.

While the NFT craze of 2021 can now be seen as a classic bubble, many of those who invested in it have moved on to memecoins and other forms of fungible cryptocurrency, according to Ben Charoenwong.

"Overall, I think the market did not reject blockchains; it rejected non-fungibility," he states.

At the time of the craze, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates said NFT popularity was "100% based on the greater fool theory," the idea being that one can make money through the purchase of overvalued, fundamentally worthless assets as long as there is a"greater fool" willing to pay even more.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most famous NFT collections was the Bored Ape Yacht Club, a series of drawings of apes in various locations in various states of boredom. "Obviously, expensive digital images of monkeys are going to improve the world immensely," Gates joked.

In a recent development, in many ways, that collection's current status epitomizes NFTs' fall from grace better than anything else. Although it remains one of the biggest NFT marketplaces, its value has plunged.

The singer Justin Bieber bought one image for 500 ETH (Ethereum), or around $1.3 million dollars. The value fell by around 99% to around $14,000. He still owns it.

Yet the fact that these images still command such prices shows they are not entirely worthless. That offers some hope to those who still believe in the technology. Alongside other possible applications linked to AI and tokenization, NFTs may still have a future, albeit a more modest one than when they first came to public attention.

The top 10 goalscorers in Europe in the 2020s: Mbappe vs Haaland for top spot, Salah 5th…

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Which players have scored the most goals in Europe’s top five leagues in the 2020s?
  • The 2010s were dominated by Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo, but neither are playing in Europe anymore and didn’t get enough goals before they left to stay in the top 10 scorers of the decade.
  • There are plenty of familiar names in the current top 10 though, with the two leading scorers separated by just four goals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Which players have scored the most goals in Europe’s top five leagues in the 2020s?

The 2010s were dominated by Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo, but neither are playing in Europe anymore and didn’t get enough goals before they left to stay in the top 10 scorers of the decade.

There are plenty of familiar names in the current top 10 though, with the two leading scorers separated by just four goals.

Here are the 10 players with the most goals across the Premier League, La Liga, Serie A, Bundesliga and Ligue 1 since the turn of the decade.

Schick knocked ex-Aston Villa striker Ollie Watkins out of the top 10 in October.

He began the 2020s on loan at RB Leipzig from Roma, but went on to find his home at Leverkusen, where’s he’s now closing in on 100 league goals.

Alexander Isak is catching up with him, but Schick is just ahead for now.

After emerging in European football with a prolific spell at Gent, David joined Lille in the summer of 2020.

Over the next five seasons in Ligue 1, 87 goals by the Canada international followed.

He found things a bit tougher in Serie A after joining Juventus in 2025, only scoring six times from 36 league outings so far.

Juventus have sent him on loan to Atletico Madrid for this season and he scored on his La Liga debut.

Arguably the least household name here, Budimir plays for Osasuna and has only ever made it to the play-off rounds of a European competition (the 2023-24 Conference League).

But the 41-cap, seven-goal Croatia international has showcased his reliability in La Liga over the past few seasons, hitting double figures in 2020-21, 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26.

Only Kylian Mbappe and Robert Lewandowski – spoiler alert, but those are two names you’ll be seeing again later – outscored Budimir in La Liga in the 2024-25 season. Then in 2025-26, only Mbappe and the relegated Mallorca frontman Vedat Muriqi scored more.

Now 35, Budimir might not have too much time left at the top level, but is under contract with Osasuna for the rest of the season.

Now 30 years old, Guirassy has played exclusively in France and Germany during his career so far.

He began the 2020s in Ligue 1 with Amiens, but suffered relegation at the end of the 2019-20 season before moving back into the top flight with Rennes.

Whilst with Rennes, he added another 19 Ligue 1 goals to his five from the second half of 2019-20.

A move to Germany with Stuttgart followed in 2022, leading to 39 Bundesliga goals in two years. He came one shy of reaching the same amount from his first two seasons with Borussia Dortmund.

Martinez has been with Inter Milan since the summer of 2018, which means his debut season in Serie A was the only one that didn’t span into any of the 2020s.

It was also the only one in which he has failed to hit double figures of goals. The Argentine striker even enjoyed three consecutive seasons with 20+ goals between 2021-22 and 2023-24, ranking as Serie A’s top scorer for the latter.

Martinez has often played as part of a strike partnership at Inter, but his longevity enables him to outrank colleagues past and present like Romelu Lukaku, Edin Dzeko and Marcus Thuram for goals since the start of the decade.

Salah left Liverpool in the summer for Trabzonspor, marking the end (for now) of his goal-getting in Europe’s top leagues.

He was extraordinary in front of goal after joining Liverpool in 2017, being able to boast 128 Premier League goals in the 2020s alone.

During that time, he claimed two Golden Boots, including from the 2024-25 season when Liverpool won the league.

He should be staying in this top 10 long after his departure from Liverpool thanks to the collection of goals he has already built up.

Lewandowski denied Erling Haaland the chance to win a Golden Boot in the Bundesliga while maintaining outlandish levels of form for Bayern Munich.

In a recent development, lewandowski then began firing them in for Barcelona, where he moved in 2022. More than 80 La Liga goals followed.

Now at the age of 38, Lewandowski only scored 14 times in the league last season, but has proven wrong anyone who may have doubted his ability to keep scoring regularly at this stage of his career.

The winner of the European Golden Shoe in each of his last two seasons with Bayern, Lewandowski was La Liga’s top scorer in his first with Barcelona.

He is now playing outside of Europe for Chicago Fire in MLS.

Kane has 99 Bundesliga goals to his name from 97 games since joining Bayern Munich in 2023 and was top of this ranking by the end of last season.

Before his spell with Bayern, he enjoyed some prolific seasons towards the end of his time in the Premier League with Tottenham Hotspur, including 30 in his last season.

The 33-year-old is in the final season of his contract with Bayern but is showing no signs of slowing down, even breaking the 60-goal barrier in all competitions last season.

Haaland is still behind Salah in the Premier League scoring chart for the 2020s, but his exploits in the Bundesliga with Borussia Dortmund from the start of the decade place him 50-odd goals above the Liverpool legend here.

Haaland entered Europe’s top five leagues by joining Dortmund in January 2020 and proceeded to score 62 Bundesliga goals from 67 games prior to his move to Manchester City.

The massive Norwegian striker was in no mood to slow his scoring rate in England, setting a fresh Premier League record for most goals in a 38-game season at the first time of asking with 36 (from just 35 appearances).

Haaland shattered through the landmark of 100 Premier League goals during the 2025-26 season and at the age of 26, should still have plenty more goals up his sleeve in the years to come.

Mbappe will most likely be going toe to toe with Haaland over the next few years to finish in top spot.

By the time he left PSG in 2024, Mbappe had become the French club’s all-time record scorer. A move to Real Madrid followed and he went on to score a Pichichi-worthy 31 goals in his first La Liga season.

Industry observers note that mbappe finished with 25 to his name in his second – again being La Liga’s top scorer – which meant he was recently able to pass a half-century of La Liga goals. He will be hungry for more (and silverware) over the coming seasons.

Martin O’Neill has told Oliver Sorensen that it’s now time for him to deliver in a Celtic jersey.

The Danish midfielder arrived in Glasgow with a massive reputation after coming in on a one-year loan from Parma. But in his seven appearances to date, the 24-year-old has failed to show why the Italian club paid Midtjylland £8.4million for his services a year ago.

‘I think that he also arrived late as well, trying to get to know people, trying to get his position, trying to get up to speed with what we do. And whatever we do, I bet you it’ll be something really different to what he was doing at Parma.

‘Because nobody’s made it after having lost the first three games. So, the next two matches are vital for us.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • George Whitesides at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts, where he spent most of his academic career.Credit: Rick Friedman/Corbis via Getty.
  • George Whitesides, a towering figure in chemistry who pushed chemists to cross boundaries to solve global problems, died on 19 November.
  • His son George, a US congressman representing California, confirmed Whitesides’s passing on the social media platform X, saying that the chemist died at home surrounded by family.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

George Whitesides at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts, where he spent most of his academic career.Credit: Rick Friedman/Corbis via Getty.

George Whitesides, a towering figure in chemistry who pushed chemists to cross boundaries to solve global problems, died on 19 November. He was 87.

His son George, a US congressman representing California, confirmed Whitesides’s passing on the social media platform X, saying that the chemist died at home surrounded by family.

Meet the soft, cuddly robots of the future.

Meet the soft, cuddly robots of the future.

In a recent development, whitesides made landmark contributions to many fields: he was a pioneer in patterning surfaces with molecules, a technique that enabled ‘lab on a chip’ diagnostic devices, advances in nanotechnology and more. He prided himself on switching research interests often, telling students, “If somebody else is working on something, don’t work on it.”.

Industry observers note that following the news of the chemist’s passing, messages celebrating his impact flooded online platforms. “I am so saddened to hear of his passing,” Zhenan Bao, a chemical engineer at Stanford University in California, wrote on LinkedIn. “George showed us that the most notable problems don’t respect the lines between disciplines. He moved freely across chemistry, materials, biology, and engineering.”.

Whitesides trained hundreds of scientists who came through his laboratory, first at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and then at Harvard University, both in Cambridge. But he also inspired many others, notes Joseph DeSimone, a polymer scientist at Stanford. In traditional chemistry departments, “there’s often a lot of pressure to stay in your lane, and he made it okay not to. In fact, he made it exciting not to”, DeSimone says.

Industry observers note that whitesides was born in Louisville, Kentucky, in 1939. One of his first experiences with chemistry was as a teenager, cleaning glassware at his father’s chemical engineering firm in his hometown.

After a bachelor’s degree in chemistry at Harvard, he enroled for a PhD at California Institute of Technology in Pasadena, studying how the workhorse chemicals known as Grignard reagents form and behave.

By 1963, Whitesides became a faculty member at MIT, where he would switch to studying the fundamentals of self-assembled monolayers (SAMs)1. These are tightly packed coatings of organic compounds that are a single-molecule thick, formed spontaneously because of forces drawing the molecules to a surface and to one another.

According to recent reports, george Whitesides and his research group pioneered low-cost, paper-based microfluidic 'lab-on-a-chip' devices. Credit: Volker Steger/Science Photo Library.

From there, Whitesides saw ways of using SAMs to easily and cheaply create patterned surfaces — which at the time were often made with complicated lithography techniques involving light and ‘stencils’. He would go on to invent soft lithography2, which instead uses polymer stamps to transfer micro- and nanoscopic patterns of molecules to surfaces.

Sources indicate that this became an “enabling” research tool, states John Rogers, a materials scientist at Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois, who was a postdoc with Whitesides at Harvard. The ability to easily pattern surfaces opened the door to creating 3D nanostructures, microfluidics and much more. It also “democratized” the ability to do this type of research, Rogers adds, because you no longer needed sophisticated cleanroom facilities and etching techniques to create such materials.

One of two survivors from that team is Jan Oblak who has racked up 555 appearances for Atleti.

He is still only 33, no age for a goalkeeper, and remains first choice. He looks set to stay for at least two more years as well with his contract expiring in 2028.

The right back left Atleti in 2019 to move to Brazil and Sao Paulo where he spent two seasons before retiring in 2020.

Industry observers note that since retiring, he has become a business owner and pundit. He appears on the Spanish version of DAZN and is CEO of Red Thunder Sports, a sports event agency.

The hardman centre-back is still playing even at the age of 35.

After retiring from playing in 2023, he cut his managerial teeth at his final employer Flamengo in their youth setup.

In 2024, he was given the top job and won the Copa do Brasil, the Carioca, the Supercopa do Brasil, the Copa Libertadores and Serie A but life comes at you fast and he was sacked in March 2026 following a poor start to the season.

According to recent reports, that did little to dent his reputation though and he picked up his next job at Monaco. His team are at the moment seventh in Ligue 1, five points off leaders PSG.

The fall of Saul is one nobody would have seen coming back in 2016.

A year later, he would sign a nine-year contract that was scheduled to end this past summer, but even at the time, he was suffering from a kidney matter that would soon disrupt his career.

During a match against Bayer Leverkusen in 2015, Saul collided with Kyriakos Papadopoulos and had what the Atletico president declared a “destroyed” kidney.

He ignored doctors’ advice to keep going, playing with a catheter, but it all caught up with him. He failed to nail down a position in Simeone’s side and soon fell out of favour.

He moved to Chelsea in one of the more forgettable loan deals and even after he looked to be back in the Atletico first team, he was back on loan in 2024, this time to Sevilla.

His stint with Atletico ended permanently in 2025 when he left Europe to join Flamengo in Brazil where he remains to this day at the age of 32.

After his time in Madrid, he moved to Chinese club Beijing Renhe before returning to Spain in 2020, this time at second division side Cadiz.

Since retiring in 2021, not much has been heard from Fernandez who appears to be enjoying the quiet life back in his native Argentina.

The captain that season is now on the sidelines as one of Simeone’s assistants.

His path there goes from leaving Atletico in 2018 to join Qatari side Al Sadd before hanging up his boots in 2020.

Gabi began his coaching career in charge of Getafe’s youth team but took over the B team in November 2023.

According to recent reports, in 2025, he was named Zaragoza boss and helped the club avoid relegation to the third division. After a poor start the following year, he was sacked.

In the summer, he returned to Madrid to become Simeone’s assistant, replacing former Arsenal man Nelson Vivas.

Ten years on and Koke is still part of the Atletico squad.

He’s the club record appearance holder by some distance – 752 to Oblak’s 555 – and is about as much of a club legend as you can be.

He’s a one-club man, joining Atleti as a kid in 2000 and signing an extension in the summer.

Torres was on loan at Atletico when they reached the Champions League final but he rejoined permanently in the summer, staying until 2019 when he left for Japanese side Sagan Tosu.

Either a beloved club legend or a turncoat depending on how you view his Barcelona move.

Breaking: Germany's celebrated children's author Janosch has died

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (831 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Janosch, the pen name of German author and illustrator Horst Eckert, won hearts around the world with his warm and simple sense of humor.
  • Janosch created more than 150 books, which have been translated into over 30 languages.
  • His best-selling children's book, "Oh, wie schön ist Panama," translated into English as "The Trip to Panama," was so lucrative that Janosch was able to settle down on the Canary Island of Tenerife in 1980, where he lived together with his wife Ines.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Janosch, the pen name of German author and illustrator Horst Eckert, won hearts around the world with his warm and simple sense of humor. He charmed children and adults alike with his iconic Tiger, Bear, Tiger-Duck and other animals.

Janosch created more than 150 books, which have been translated into over 30 languages.

His best-selling children's book, "Oh, wie schön ist Panama," translated into English as "The Trip to Panama," was so lucrative that Janosch was able to settle down on the Canary Island of Tenerife in 1980, where he lived together with his wife Ines. The writer and illustrator died peacefully at the age of 95, his publisher Bernhard Feil revealed on Wednesday.

Janosch was born as Horst Eckert on March 11, 1931, in Hindenburg (now Zabrze, Poland) in what was then Upper Silesia. After World War II, his family had to flee to Germany.

Sources indicate that in 1953, Janosch started studying at the Academy of Art in Munich, thinking that it would be easy to become an artist. He was however dismissed after just a few terms for "lack of talent.".

According to recent reports, but luckily for his later readers, Janosch did not give up. He continued to work as a freelance artist, soon discovering his second great gift, namely writing.

His first children's book about a horse named Valek was published in 1960.

Although Janosch became famous primarily for his children's books, he also wrote books for adults that focused on his own childhood.

Sources indicate that even though he wrote cheerful books for children, Janosch hardly had any positive memories of his own childhood, as his father was an alcoholic. He was beaten not only by him but also by his mother and grandmother. Raised in a strictly Catholic environment, he was continuously threatened to be punished by God.

Later on, Janosch tried to overcome the burden of his childhood memories by turning to alcohol as well.

Industry observers note that he always expressed a great deal of understanding for children, trying to encourage them to stand up for their rights. As a result of his childhood experiences, Janosch did not want to have children himself, and his attitude towards the Catholic Church always remained divided. "As I am a sinner and a heretic, God will let me live a long life so that I can return to the Church," he told his biographer Angela Bajorek.

Janosch's animal figures are endearing but not always well-behaved. They love all kinds of nonsense. But even if they lie to each other or put their own interests first, the true winner at the end of stories is always friendship and solidarity.

Janosch achieved his major breakthrough with "The Trip to Panama," a story about two friends, a little tiger and a bear, who set out to find their paradise in Panama. After touring around in circles, they finally end up where they started out; they realize that their journey was the destination. Janosch received the German Youth Book Prize in 1979 for the work.

Recent findings suggest that janosch's protagonists have become familiar to generations of children all over the world. They come up over and over again in the various stories carefully illustrated with water colors.

There is the honest lion Hans from the toy chest who fails to catch a nutcracker with his lies. There is Schnuddel and a ridiculous bragger Günter the Box-Frog. And then there is a tiger that collects mushrooms while looking out for his devoted friend, a bear, who always stands up for him even when the tiger temporarily leaves him because of a little pig in one of the stories.

In a recent development, the "Tigerente," literally "Tiger-Duck," a wooden duck on wheels with yellow-brown stripes, appears on numerous pictures by the illustrator. At times, the animal has been tossed into a corner, at times it is hanging from the ceiling, or the Box-Frog pulls it across the drawing.

His iconic figures, especially the Tiger-Duck, have served as motifs on various items, from cups to stamps to jewelry, and even on airplanes. Film adaptations and TV series based on his stories were produced in German and English.

Recent findings suggest that guests who visited Janosch in Tenerife were impressed by his very modest lifestyle. He always noted that hanging around in his hammock doing nothing was what he enjoyed most. And yet Janosch remained very active until the end of his life.

From 2013 to 2019, he wrote a column for the German weekly Die Zeit, taking on the role of Mr. Wondrak, who commented on world affairs. Shortly before his 90th birthday in 2021, the complete collection of his Mr. Wondrak columns were published as a book in German.

Like the protagonists in his stories, Janosch always tried to content himself with few things. As he wrote in one of his books: "He who needs almost nothing, has everything.".

This article was originally written in German.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

German carmaker BMW reported a nearly 15% drop in third-quarter net profit on Wednesday, as competition from China shakes the global car industry.

Net profit for the third quarter fell to 1.45 billion euros ($1.61 billion), while sales fell nearly 6% to 30.45 billion euros, BMW said.

Recent findings suggest that the main cause of the decline was BMW's poor business in China. Although the company sold more cars in the US and Europe compared to the same period last year, this could only partially offset the decline in China.

BMW's car deliveries in China, which were already at their lowest level since 2017 last year, fell 24.8% in the quarter and consequently dragged global deliveries down by 6.3.

CEO Milan Nedeljkovic mentioned his company would "specifically intensify and accelerate structural measures.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

BMW on Tuesday also lowered its outlook for the current year, citing the faster-than-planned implementation of restructuring measures that includes 8,000 layoffs in its home market.

German carmakers have been struggling to compete with their Chinese counterparts in the electric vehicle market,  resulting in cost-cutting measures.

Volkswagen, the world's second-largest carmaker, is battling mounting competition from falling demand in its core Chinese market.

BMW, and its industry heavyweight peers, Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz, have revealed plans to scale back production and reduce costs.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The Volkswagen Group posted its worst quarterly results in more than a decade earlier this October.

It is looking to cut about 15% of its workforce worldwide, or 100,000 jobs, by the end of the decade. BMW has confirmed that it will cut up to 8,000 jobs — about 5% of its workforce — by the end of 2027.

On the other hand, German auto parts supplier Schaeffler confirmed on Tuesday that it planned to cut almost 3,500 jobs and close five sites in Europe, by 2028.

According to the firm statement, three-fourths of the 3,460 job cuts and four of the five site closures will be in Germany.

German automotive supplier Bosch, the world's biggest, confirmed last year that it would cut 13,000 jobs, mostly in its auto division.

Leading ice hockey nations, sponsors oppose Russia's return
