💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that since its inception in 1990, the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship has almost always been held in the spring — apart from 2021 and 2022, when the COVID-19 pandemic saw it moved to the summer.
  • According to recent reports, the idea is make it easier for all of the world's best players to participate.
  • Recent findings suggest that "This gives the women's game a unique selling point," International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) President Franz Reindl recently told the SID news agency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that since its inception in 1990, the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship has almost always been held in the spring — apart from 2021 and 2022, when the COVID-19 pandemic saw it moved to the summer. This year, though, the tournament, being hosted by Denmark from November 6 to November 16, is being held in November for the first time.

According to recent reports, the idea is make it easier for all of the world's best players to participate. Since its inception in 2023, the North America-based Professional Women's Hockey League (PWHL), widely considered the world's best, has had to pause its season to allow players to take part in the Worlds. This is no longer necessary, as the PWHL's regular season doesn't open until December.

Recent findings suggest that "This gives the women's game a unique selling point," International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) President Franz Reindl recently told the SID news agency. "Because the PWHL season begins after this, we can be certain that the very best players are participating.".

Previously, the teams were divided into a stronger group and a weaker group, with the idea being to avoid, as much as possible, lopsided scores. This is because women's hockey is not as balanced as the men's game, with Canada or the United States having won every tournament since its inception.

Sources indicate that under the old system, all five teams in the stronger Group A advanced to the quarterfinals. Under the latest format, four of the five teams advance from both groups. This also sees powerhouses the US and Canada in separate groups, meaning the marquee matchup can't occur early in the tournament.

Group A: USA, Czechia, Switzerland, Germany, Austria.

Group B: Canada, Finland, Sweden, Japan, Denmark.

Sources indicate that no. While the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled on October 30 — a week before the opening faceoff of the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship — that the IIHF must allow Russia back into its tournaments during the 2026-2027 season, it made no mention of this tournament. Under the CAS ruling though, the IIHF will be required to include Russia at the 2027 tournament in Quebec City.

Sources indicate that as noted above, either Canada or the United States has won every edition of this tournament — and indeed the two countries have split Olympic gold medals between them (Canada with five, USA with three) since the sport was introduced to the Winter Games in 1998. There is nothing to suggest that this is about to change in Herning and Esbjerg, although Canada enters the tournament with a vastly different roster from the one that won Olympic silver in Milano in February.

Among those looking to break this North American domination are Finland, the only other team ever to have made it to a world championship final and Switzerland, who took bronze in Milan.

The United States and Canada will play in generic kits provided by the International Ice Hockey Federation's official supplier due to an ongoing commercial rights dispute.

Sources indicate that the Canadian federation, Hockey Canada, said in a statement on Wednesday that its players would be wearing jerseys designed by True Hockey instead of their Bauer jerseys featuring the national team logo. USA Hockey has confirmed that its players too will be wearing jerseys without its national emblem.

"While we have yet to see the jersey Canada will be playing in on Friday, our team remains focused on the tournament and representing our country proudly on and off the ice," Hockey Canada said.

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Chelsea, who start the day in fifth, and 16th-placed Manchester United at Stamford Bridge. On Sunday and Monday it seemed certain that Michael Carrick would be relieved of his duties before today’s game but has survived for now, hoping to turn things around in the no man’s land that sometimes resembles a vote of confidence and at others a stay of execution.

Thirty years ago when Newcastle United were coming off the bridle in the title race with Manchester United, Alex Ferguson, as he then was, accused a Leeds team, who had been in freefall since the new year, of professional malpractice when they put in a rare display of passionate commitment and tenacity at Old Trafford in a 1-0 defeat.

“Why are they not in the top six?” asked Ferguson. “To me they’re cheating their manager. You wait and see the difference when they play Newcastle.” The hate between the Leeds and Manchester united fanbases was such, he implied, that they had decided to put a shift in because, for once, they feared the consequences if they had not. It seems to this observer that the boot is now on the other foot. These Manchester United players roused themselves to fight at Elland Road then chucked it in against Como and Bournemouth. If that’s not “cheating their manager”, what is?

Carrick will have to hope that some of the old hostility between Chelsea and Manchester United might encourage the players to run about a bit this afternoon and, at the very least, get stuck in rather than crumple spinelessly as they did last week. I doubt it would be enough to save Carrick’s job in the medium term but at least it would address whether they could stake a claim to be part of the rebuilding process.

Recent findings suggest that as for Chelsea, who were awful in defeat by Brentford and Spurs either side of impressive victories over Bournemouth and at Everton, they need to find some defensive solidity, discipline and a way of terrorising defences in the absence of Joao Pedro. They are a work in progress still, in the fifth year of the hedge fund hegemony. For all that attacking talent and Moises Caicedo’s ability to steamroll midfielders, their defence does not inspire confidence and last year’s petulance continues to simmer.

Preparing for 45C: How Germany tests its crisis response

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (758 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Imagine a situation in which prolonged drought has devastated Germany and much of Europe, taking a toll on people's lives, the environment and economy — with a heat wave with temperatures of up to 45 degrees Celsius (113 degrees Fahrenheit) compounding the situation.
  • About 180 organizations across Germany, including more than 60 ministries at the state level and nearly 20 federal authorities, are taking part in a major crisis exercise known as LÜKEX 26, which is built around this very scenario.
  • According to recent reports, it is Germany's cross-government crisis management exercise organized by the Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance (BBK).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine a situation in which prolonged drought has devastated Germany and much of Europe, taking a toll on people's lives, the environment and economy — with a heat wave with temperatures of up to 45 degrees Celsius (113 degrees Fahrenheit) compounding the situation.

About 180 organizations across Germany, including more than 60 ministries at the state level and nearly 20 federal authorities, are taking part in a major crisis exercise known as LÜKEX 26, which is built around this very scenario.

According to recent reports, it is Germany's cross-government crisis management exercise organized by the Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance (BBK). And it's been up and running for more than two decades.

According to recent reports, the first LÜKEX in 2004 dealt with the scenario of an extreme winter with a major power outage. Lessons from that exercise proved valuable in 2005 when the Münsterland region of North Rhine-Westphalia — Germany's most populous state — experienced the worst power outage in the country's postwar history. When heavy snowfall caused power lines to collapse, leaving 250,000 people without electricity for days, there was a better understanding of who to contact and where the bottlenecks were.

According to recent reports, since it first started, LÜKEX has trained for scenarios involving terror attacks, an influenza pandemic, biological health threats, storm floods in northern Germany and gas shortages in southern Germany. The most recent exercise in 2023 simulated a cyberattack targeting government operations.

With the help of other ministries, the German Weather Service and the Federal Institute of Hydrology, the BBK developed a drought risk analysis to serve as the scenario.

Participants, which include aid organizations Malteser and the German Red Cross, didn't know the specifics of the challenges they would be facing until the exercise kicked off on Wednesday.

Recent findings suggest that at that point, they were told it was July 20, 2027. In that simulated future, they find themselves in a Germany that has been struggling with extreme heat for weeks; water levels in rivers are falling, food supplies are becoming scarce and emergency services are under growing pressure.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that patrick Pöhler, spokesperson for Malteser, said additional details include supermarkets having run out of water, collapsed supply chains and skyrocketing prices to enter a swimming pool. He said the scenario also goes into how the situation is impacting sections of society.

Recent findings suggest that "Emergency services and elderly care are areas that require particular attention," Pöhler said. "The increasingly extreme summers of recent years have shown how severely heat can affect staffing levels and operational capacity.".

In its scenario, the northern port city of Hamburg is tasked with managing the disruption of key transport routes that are impacting access to food and drinking water, as well as handling disinformation attacks that are fueling public fear.

It has been revealed that "We have not conducted an exercise of this magnitude since the end of the Cold War. Yet such preparations are essential to strengthen our resilience and crisis-response capabilities," noted Hamburg's minister for the interior, Andy Grote.

LÜKEX is designed to test and strengthen the country's ability to manage major crises at a strategic level. No matter the specific scenario, they all help test internal structures, workflows and decision-making processes.

"The lessons learned are continuously incorporated into improving preparedness, planning and cooperation in civil protection," stated BBK spokesperson Katharina Böcker.

In a recent development, this year's topic was decided a long time ago, well before recent summers in which Germany experienced extreme heat, she added. Thousands of people died from heat-related causes during the hot months of this year.

"Crises such as extreme heat waves and prolonged droughts can affect large parts of the population and challenge the operational capabilities of our critical structures over an extended period," said Christian Reuter, secretary general of the German Red Cross, another organization taking part.

Observers take note of how organizations react in the crisis scenario to find out what went well and where things didn't run smoothly.

"We are explicitly encouraged to make mistakes," said Malteser's Pöhler, because that is how weaknesses can be identified and addressed.

A first internal debrief is scheduled for Friday, he added.

A preliminary report with the main findings and respective recommendations is due to be published in the first quarter of next year. A full evaluation report will then be released later in the third quarter of 2027.

#118272. Continuous N-to-C Peptide Synthesis

Continuous N-to-C Peptide Synthesis

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (597 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, current state-of-the-art peptide synthesis faces a significant global challenge in efficiency and sustainability.1 With demand for peptide therapeutics growing rapidly,2,3 our ability to provide these important medicines is under increasing pressure.4 Chemical synthesis typically proceeds C-to-N and requires protecting groups, whereas ribosomal synthesis proceeds N-to-C from unprotected amino acids (AAs).
  • This is a preview of subscription content, access via your institution.
  • Access Nature and 54 other Nature Portfolio journals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, current state-of-the-art peptide synthesis faces a significant global challenge in efficiency and sustainability.1 With demand for peptide therapeutics growing rapidly,2,3 our ability to provide these important medicines is under increasing pressure.4 Chemical synthesis typically proceeds C-to-N and requires protecting groups, whereas ribosomal synthesis proceeds N-to-C from unprotected amino acids (AAs). To improve efficiency and sustainability, we developed a continuous N-to-C Peptide Synthesis (NCPS) using N-/C-unprotected AAs or fragments without intermediate isolations, achieving ≥95% average yield per coupling and ≤1.0% epimerization. The method enabled seven consecutive couplings. Starting from N-/C-unprotected AAs, peptide assembly requires fewer isolations than those needed to prepare the corresponding Fmoc-AA building blocks before conventional synthesis can begin. This method accepts all 20 canonical AAs and a wide range of non-canonical AAs important for drug-like profiles.5 Longer peptides can be readily assembled through continuous fragment coupling while maintaining chiral integrity. This approach reduces isolations by ~10-fold and waste generation by up to ~100-fold. We further developed a flow synthesizer that enhances speed and productivity while mitigating batch manufacturing risks. The method enabled the synthesis of a tirzepatide heptapeptide fragment, degarelix, a 14-mer engineered macrocyclic peptide, and semaglutide. Overall, continuous NCPS has the potential to transform peptide manufacturing.

Tesla to 'wind down' production of flop Cybertruck

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla owner Elon Musk noted on Friday that the tech giant would scale down production of the Cybertruck at its Austin factory in the coming year.
  • The South African entrepreneur mentioned Tesla would be scaling back production of his futuristic but often-mocked pickup truck and amping up production of what he hopes will soon become a fleet of fully automated taxis.
  • "Tesla will be winding down production of the cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk said on his X social media site.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla owner Elon Musk noted on Friday that the tech giant would scale down production of the Cybertruck at its Austin factory in the coming year.

The South African entrepreneur mentioned Tesla would be scaling back production of his futuristic but often-mocked pickup truck and amping up production of what he hopes will soon become a fleet of fully automated taxis.

"Tesla will be winding down production of the cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk said on his X social media site.

The announcement follows a bruising week for Musk amid the US midterm elections, where Republicans struggled despite his major donations, with his companies losing billions in value by market capitalization as investors sought to ditch stock.

Musk later responded to a complimentary user online who hailed the Cybertruck as the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made," and calling it an "end of an era" by saying: "True.".

For years he had poured much of his enthusiastic marketing zeal into promoting the Cybertruck, saying during the 2023 launch "finally, the future will look like the future.".

However the oversized body, straight lines and stainless steel and the post-apocalpytic vibe these created also met with widespread criticism and even mockery.

The electric powertrain was probably a barrier to sales in the US, by far the biggest pickup truck market, where Musk had hoped to take on some of the country's top-selling gas-guzzling vehicles like the Ford F150 or the Chevrolet Silverado and the Dodge Ram.

Meanwhile, the car's striking shape, weight and size made it impossible for Tesla to try to crack Europe, where electric vehicles are gaining a much larger market share.

Sources indicate that unlike in the US, EU safety regulations place considerable emphasis not just on people in cars in accidents, but also on the dangers posed to pedestrians who might be hit by a vehicle. That meant it was not possible for Tesla to register and sell the Cybertruck for road use in Europe.

Beyond this, the vehicle's size would likely have rendered it impractical and unpopular on many European roads, where space tends to be at more of a premium.

Depending how quick the wind-down proves to be, the Cybertruck's production run could prove shorter than its five-year R&D phase.

Given its longstanding complications meeting Musk's very public sales and production predictions, Tesla does not publish sales figures broken down by model.

But according to the automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the company sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down from 38,965 in 2024.

At launch in 2023, Musk had predicted unit sales nearer a quarter of a million.

It has been revealed that for orientation, Ford sold more than 800,000 F-Series pickups in the US last year, a slight boost on 2024's numbers. These vehicles start at less than half the list price of a Cybertruck in the US.

Industry observers note that the IPO for SpaceX this year revealed that Musk's second-largest tech giant was comfortably the biggest buyer of Cybertrucks in 2025. It bought vehicles worth $131 million and did not even enjoy a bulk-buy or friends-rate discount, paying list prices for the fleet.

The Cybercab is a vehicular element in Musk's bid to transform Tesla towards a organization focused more on AI and robotics than automobilies.

Rather than just featuring the self-drive or driving assistance programs that Musk has been championing for years, the Cybercab has no steering wheels, pedals or mirrors at all and is designed never to have a human in control.

Musk say the model will be the firm's main autonomous model and will supply a global network of Robotaxis.

In a recent development, starting in the past few months, around 300 such vehicles have been registered and have started operating, on approved roads in the Austin area near Tesla's Gigafactory Texas. They're being added to the existing fleet of autonomous Model Y Teslas being used for the purpose, serving in an area known as a geofence of around 680 square kilometers (264 square miles).

Tech Report: Amid protests, France's rising debt costs threaten stability

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (998 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.
  • If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.
  • France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.

If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.

France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). By comparison, Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly 65%, despite its €600 billion investment package for infrastructure and defense.

Germany still enjoys the highest possible AAA credit rating. France, by contrast, is rated AA, A+ or Aa3, depending on the credit agency. While Germany's outlook is consistently rated as stable, several agencies have assigned France a negative outlook.

Sources indicate that as a result, the French government must pay higher interest rates on its borrowing than Berlin. The risk premium over German government bonds, known as the spread, is now at its highest level since the financial crisis. France pays nearly 1.6 percentage points more in interest than Germany on 10-year bonds.

The spread acts as a kind of "fever gauge" for bond markets, explained Friedrich Heinemann, an economist at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW) in Mannheim.

"This fever gauge then forces a change of course. If the spread rises too sharply, France's financing conditions come under pressure, and anyone in France who needs a loan has to pay higher interest rates. Banks then get into trouble, and the crisis escalates further," Heinemann told DW.

"This could then slide toward a financial crisis, which would finally send a clear signal to everyone: Things cannot continue like this unless you are prepared to risk a genuine economic collapse," he said.

Landry Charrier, a researcher at the University of Bonn's Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies, however, does not expect France's debt-fueled spending spree to end anytime soon.

Recent findings suggest that "French people are aware of the country's high public debt. But debt remains an abstract concept if its consequences are barely felt in everyday life. According to INSEE [the French national statistics agency — Editor's note], 56% of the population receive more in government benefits and services than they pay in taxes and social contributions. The majority therefore have a tangible interest in maintaining the status quo," Charrier told DW.

For more than half a century, France has regularly spent more than it collects in tax revenue. The last time it balanced its national budget was in 1974.

Recent findings suggest that france last paid a similarly high-risk premium at the end of 2011, during the eurozone debt crisis. What is particularly striking is how rapidly it has risen: Since June 2026, the spread over German government bonds has more than doubled.

The main driver is not so much the general level of interest rates. Rather, it's the growing risk premium investors demand in response to high debt levels, political instability, large budget deficits and the recent unrest.

The higher the interest rates, the larger the share of the national budget that must be devoted to debt servicing alone. France is expected to pay more than €79 billion in interest on its total public debt in 2026. That figure is projected to exceed €91 billion in 2027 and could reach between €125 billion and €132 billion by 2030.

According to recent reports, these figures include the costs incurred by social security funds and local authorities. The central government's interest bill alone is currently estimated at €62.6 billion by the Agence France Tresor, a French Treasury agency.

According to recent reports, in the coming years, France will have to refinance large amounts of outstanding bonds that were issued when interest rates were at historic lows. At the same time, the country's substantial budget deficit means it must take on additional debt.

Recent findings suggest that the trend of rising interest costs is also affecting Germany. The ZEW's Heinemann has calculated that German interest payments are likely to increase sharply by the early 2030s.

Industry observers note that "For the federal government alone, which has so far paid around €30 billion, the figure will triple within a few years as both debt and interest rates rise. And it won't stop there — it will exceed €90 billion. Reaching €100 billion in annual interest payments in the federal budget is then no longer far off," warned the economist.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In France, however, economic realities seem to have little impact on political debate. Both the far-right National Rally (RN) and the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) are campaigning on costly promises.

Industry observers note that RN leader Marine Le Pen, for example, wants to reinstate the retirement age of 62 while promising €140 billion in savings. Jean-Luc Melenchon, LFI's leader, has even suggested that government bonds held by the French central bank should be "thrown into the fire.".

"Nobody will ever notice they've disappeared," he has claimed.

For Heinemann, this is "a good example of radical parties on both the right and the left simply telling economic fairy tales.".

Their common message, he said, is that "there is a way out of this mess that requires neither fiscal consolidation nor painful cuts.".

Charrier is convinced that many French people have yet to grasp the seriousness of the situation.

"The euro has made it easier for France to access cheap financing and has long softened the pressure to adjust," he pointed out.

Industry observers note that "In the past, currency devaluations [of the French franc — Editor's note] made economic imbalances immediately felt through declining purchasing power and rising prices. Today, that warning signal is missing. This has created the illusion that necessary adjustments can be postponed indefinitely," Charrier stated.

This article was originally written in German.

Germany hopes to host world ice hockey championship — without Russia

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (545 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A government spokesman has stated that, despite talks with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB), the International Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) and others, the impasse caused by last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling remains.
  • Since the October 30 decision, several leading ice hockey nations — including Finland, Sweden and Czechia — have mentioned they would refrain from playing against Russia in any tournament in which it is allowed to take part.
  • The first tournament to be affected would be the Men's World Juniors, which opens in Canada in late December, followed by the IIHF's premier event, the Men's World Ice Championship, to be hosted by Germany in May.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A government spokesman has stated that, despite talks with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB), the International Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) and others, the impasse caused by last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling remains.

Since the October 30 decision, several leading ice hockey nations — including Finland, Sweden and Czechia — have mentioned they would refrain from playing against Russia in any tournament in which it is allowed to take part. Several key sponsors have also threatened to pull out, should the Russians be allowed to play.

The first tournament to be affected would be the Men's World Juniors, which opens in Canada in late December, followed by the IIHF's premier event, the Men's World Ice Championship, to be hosted by Germany in May.

Stefan Kornelius, the spokesman for Germany's government, told reporters in Berlin on Friday that talks held with various stakeholders had made clear that Russia's participation would render the hosting of the championship "practically impossible — both from a sporting and an economic perspective.".

Kornelius remarked talks would continue and the government still hoped for a diplomatic solution that would allow Germany to host the championship — as planned — in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf in May.

"Our goal must be to hold the tournaments as scheduled," he said. "However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore — through dialogue — how we can still ensure the tournament takes place.".

Following the CAS ruling that the IIHF must allow Russia to return to international play, DEB chairman Frank Lutz had conceded that Germany may be forced to consider withdrawing as championship host.

Asked at Friday's press conference whether Germany could problem visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman declined to answer categorically, but did indicate that this would be difficult under restrictions presently in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," mentioned spokesperson Martin Giese.

Earlier this week, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney categorically ruled out Russian players taking part in the World Juniors in Alberta.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he stated.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors," he said, "the Russians will not be there.".

Russian President Vladimir Putin has also weighed in on the issue, accusing countries opposing Russia's return to international sport of violating the rights of his country's athletes.

It has been revealed that the IIHF Council had originally called two days of meetings, on Monday and Tuesday, to try to reach a consensus on how to respond to the CAS decision — before extending discussions for a third day, on Thursday. By Friday, its members had evidently still not reached a consensus.

This comes as the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship, which is not affected by the CAS decision, opened in Denmark — and with the clock ticking toward the start of the World Juniors in Alberta on December 26.

Senegal KEEP Africa Cup of Nations title: Champions see crown restored in huge CAS verdict despite walking off the pitch in chaotic final against Morocco

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 09:30 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 14:47 EST, 24 November 2026.
  • Senegal have been reinstated as Africa Cup of Nations winners after succeeding with an appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS), ten months after they beat Morocco in Rabat.
  • The ruling follows a controversial final in which Senegal initially won 1-0 after extra time, only for the result to be overturned following an appeal to Confederation of African Football (CAF) by the Moroccan Football Federation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By BOBBY MANZI, FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 09:30 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 14:47 EST, 24 November 2026.

Senegal have been reinstated as Africa Cup of Nations winners after succeeding with an appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS), ten months after they beat Morocco in Rabat.

The ruling follows a controversial final in which Senegal initially won 1-0 after extra time, only for the result to be overturned following an appeal to Confederation of African Football (CAF) by the Moroccan Football Federation.

Two months after the final, the CAF appeal board ruled that Senegal had forfeited the match because their players had walked off the pitch in protest over a controversial penalty decision.

Morocco were subsequently awarded a 3-0 victory and the title. Despite that, Senegal refused to hand the trophy over.

That decision was based on Articles 82 and 84 of the AFCON regulations, which state that leaving the pitch constitutes a forfeit.

However, following an appeal to CAS, Senegal have been reinstalled as champions, with the court ruling that FIFA's law that the referee’s decision is final takes precedence over the competition regulations.

Therefore, because the officials did not enforce the competition regulations at the time, there were no grounds to overturn the result.

The Moroccan FA, though, have not given up and have vowed to take the matter beyond CAS after questioning the integrity of panelist Ulrich Haas.

The Court of Arbitration for Sport has restored Senegal as Africa Cup of Nations winners after they were successful in their appeal.

Morocco were awarded a 3-0 victory two months after the final, after it was ruled Senegal had forfeited the match by walking off the pitch in protest over a late penalty decision.

Senegal fans clashed with security in Rabat after the controversial penalty decision.

Ruling in favour of Senegal on Tuesday, CAS noted: 'In the Panel’s view, there is no doubt that the effects of the Referee’s decision were limited to the pitch.

'As such, the Panel considers that the Referee’s decision was covered by the "field of play" doctrine.

'Since Articles 82 and 84 of the AFCON Regulations are intended solely to determine the outcome of a match when a team’s conduct leads the referee to call off the game permanently, they are therefore not applicable in this case.'.

A statement from the Moroccan FA later added: 'We take note of the decision of the Court of Arbitration for Sport regarding the appeal filed by the Senegalese Football Federation against the decision of the CAF Appeals Committee, relating to the final match of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations. In this context, the Royal Moroccan Football Federation expresses its surprise and protest at the failure to take into account its demand to arrange the necessary legal consequences for practices that would compromise the integrity and credibility of the arbitration procedure, especially what has been confirmed regarding communication between the German referee Ulrich Haas (who sat on the CAS panel) and the president of the Senegalese Football Federation, 48 hours before the decision was issued.

'The Royal Moroccan Football Federation also notes that the decision did not take into account the approach recently adopted by both the International Football Association Board (IFAB) and FIFA, regarding players leaving the field of play without the referee’s permission, and the resulting disciplinary responsibilities and penalties.

'Accordingly, the Royal Moroccan Football Federation confirms its intention to pursue all available legal avenues to appeal the decision of the Court of Arbitration for Sport.'.

The chaos was triggered by events at the end of normal time, when referee Jean Jacques Ndala awarded Morocco a contentious penalty in the 98th minute after being called to the monitor by the video assistant referee to review El Hadji Malick Diouf’s challenge on Brahim Diaz.

The decision came just minutes after Senegal had seen a goal ruled out.

Furious with the penalty decision, Senegal manager Pape Thiaw instructed his players to leave the pitch in protest.

After a 17-minute delay, the team eventually returned, with former Liverpool forward Sadio Mane earning praise for remaining on the pitch and encouraging his teammates to continue.

In the dramatic aftermath, Real Madrid forward Brahim Diaz saw his Panenka penalty stopped by Senegal goalkeeper Edouard Mendy, before Ndala brought normal time to an end.

Senegal went on to score early in extra time, which has now led to a second title in the past three editions of the tournament with their 1-0 victory eventually confirmed in the courtroom.

As COP31 Antalya kicks off, can world move beyond substantial promises?

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1209 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With its pulsing music, flashy images and barrage of special effects, the key message in Antalya's marketing video is clear: Turkey, the host of the 31st edition of the UN climate talks, is cool, stylish, modern — and eco-conscious.
  • Both President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his wife, Emine, make an appearance, with Turkey's first lady calling climate change "one of the most visible manifestations of the burden human activity has placed on our planet.".
  • From November 9-20, delegates from nearly every country in the world are coming together in the Mediterranean city of Antalya to chart a way out of the climate crisis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With its pulsing music, flashy images and barrage of special effects, the key message in Antalya's marketing video is clear: Turkey, the host of the 31st edition of the UN climate talks, is cool, stylish, modern — and eco-conscious.

Both President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his wife, Emine, make an appearance, with Turkey's first lady calling climate change "one of the most visible manifestations of the burden human activity has placed on our planet.".

From November 9-20, delegates from nearly every country in the world are coming together in the Mediterranean city of Antalya to chart a way out of the climate crisis. Turkey is the official host, and Australia will lead the negotiations. But the problems they'll confront during those 12 days are far more serious than the showy marketing campaign make them out to be.

Severe drought, extreme heat, wildfires and record-low water levels in Europe's main waterways — summer across the continent was dominated by climate emergencies.

And in late August, a series of flash floods triggered by a rock-ice avalanche in Nepal and Tibet washed away entire villages, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands missing. Climate experts have linked the disaster to melting ice and a warming climate.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Globally, carbon emissions are still rising: the UN has concluded that it is no longer possible to keep global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels, the goal agreed at COP21 in 2015.

Recent findings suggest that the global transition away from polluting fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas will be at the center of attention in Antalya — once again. To date, there's been no consensus on whether and how to transition rapidly away from this main source of global warming.

Despite the setbacks, the world has made some progress thanks to the 2015 Paris Agreement.

David Victor, a climate expert at the University of California San Diego, pointed out that before then, the planet was hurtling toward an average temperature rise of between 3-3.5 C.

If current climate commitments are fully implemented, the latest UN projections show a rise of up to 2.6 C. It's a significant step forward, even though warming of that magnitude will still have worldwide consequences.

"There's no question that we could be doing more," noted Victor, though he cautioned against pinning too much on this year's summit.

All agreements at COP need to be unanimous, meaning individual states can quash any sweeping resolutions. Added to that challenge are the ongoing wars, trade conflicts and other economic problems swirling around this year's negotiations.

"It's like a giant Christmas tree in which everybody's hung their different ornaments, and the tree is groaning and more ornaments are being put on it," said Victor. "We have to look at it for what it is: It's a place where people talk about stuff.".

Instead of waiting for all COP member states to agree, Victor sees a better chance for change in what he called "clubs" — smaller alliances of governments and companies working together to advance actual solutions, whether it be in aviation, shipping or electromobility.

It has been revealed that "The Paris process is notable. It has to go forward," he told DW. "But all the work is going to be done in clubs.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

An example of this approach was last April's first ever International Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia.

Colombia and the Netherlands invited representatives from 57 countries and key sectors to discuss ways to move the world away from coal, oil and gas, after an agreement on a similar plan failed at the 2025 climate summit due to opposition from several oil-producing states.

With an eye to the ongoing trade conflicts and energy crisis, hosts Turkey and Australia have included green industrialization and the clean energy transition among their aims. One goal is to increase the share of electricity in global energy consumption to 35% by 2035, up from around 20% today.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

A recent analysis by the International Energy Agency found accelerating electrification could cut fuel-importing countries' energy bills by more than $400 billion (€357 billion) by 2035, compared to 2025 levels. The idea could appeal to regions dependent on fossil fuel imports — among them Germany and the European Union.

Ahead of COP31, German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider mentioned Germany and the EU wanted to spark upcoming momentum in the "global phaseout of fossil fuels.".

It's wouldn't just be good for the climate, but a chance for many countries to boost their economies and reduce dependence on energy imports, added Schneider in a statement.

Oil-producing states like Saudi Arabia, however, aren't interested in deals that will undermine their business model. At recent UN climate conferences, they've repeatedly blocked any final agreements, including phaseout prepares.

Even China, despite its massive expansion of wind and solar energy over the last 20 years, could be against the idea. The economic superpower traditionally rejects any outside demands, proposals or interference concerning its national decisions on energy policy.

Sources indicate that every country in the world is affected by climate change, with loss and damage calculated in the hundreds of billions from heat, drought and storms. Worst hit are vulnerable countries in the Global South and island nations, who are at risk of disappearing as sea levels rise.

That's where money comes into play, with developing countries calling for more support to protect their citizens from the harms of global warming. At the 2024 UN climate talks in Baku, Azerbaijan, industrialized nations agreed to free up at least $300 billion annually in climate financing by 2035.

But where exactly all those funds will come from remains hotly debated. At the same time, several major developed countries — most notably, the US — have cut their development aid.

The German government only paid out €4.7 billion from its 2025 budget for international climate financing, down from €6.1 billion in 2024.

"The level of financial support for developing countries today is far from what's needed," stated Jan Kowalzig, a climate expert at Oxfam Germany.

Breaking financial promises like this comes at the expense of losing the trust of developing countries and, as a result, the diplomatic power which Germany and other industrialized nations rely on to shape policy to fight climate change.

Cosima Cassel, who focuses on climate diplomacy at the independent think tank E3G in Berlin, believes Turkey's push to turbocharge electrification during an oil crisis could be successful.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

For Cassel, a successful outcome at what are expected to be difficult negotiations in Antalya would reveal actual political will behind the grand agreements.

When it comes to electrification, that means taking the expansion of electricity grids and battery storage capacity seriously — not to mention removing the barriers to further electrification.

COP31 went up in flames over fossil fuels — it sends an crucial message

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that anyone hoping for bold action on climate change has many reasons to be disappointed by the latest United Nations climate summit, COP31, which concluded in a dramatic overtime session on 22 November.
  • The last COP climate talk to break down this badly was the Copenhagen summit in 2009.
  • Sources indicate that the COP31 outcome wasn’t inevitable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that anyone hoping for bold action on climate change has many reasons to be disappointed by the latest United Nations climate summit, COP31, which concluded in a dramatic overtime session on 22 November. After gathering for nearly two weeks in the beach resort city of Antalya, Turkey, in what will probably be the hottest year on record, representatives from nearly all the world’s countries failed to agree on a proposal to tackle climate change. Almost 100 nations walked out without signing a ‘cover decision’ — a non-binding statement meant to push for ambitious action — because the document did not call on the world to transition away from fossil fuels.

The last COP climate talk to break down this badly was the Copenhagen summit in 2009. After that meeting, the late geoscientist James Lovelock commented: “I don’t think we’re yet evolved to the point where we’re clever enough to handle as complex a situation as climate change.” Seventeen years and an increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide levels of almost 40 parts per million later, and governments still seem unable to overcome national differences for the benefit of the planet.

Sources indicate that the COP31 outcome wasn’t inevitable. There had been some optimism among climate watchers ahead of the summit that, despite ongoing geopolitical conflicts, rising energy prices and energy shortages would spur countries to support a transition away from burning coal, oil and gas — the biggest drivers of climate change. But when language targeting fossil fuels disappeared from the draft cover decision after lobbying by oil-rich nations, a coalition of around 90 countries, led by the European Union and small island states, rejected the agreement.

Latest Update: 'Never Again!': Holocaust remembrance under pressure

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1293 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Young people pose inside a crematorium oven at the Buchenwald concentration camp memorial, laughing while they give the Nazi salute and take pictures of each other.
  • "Incidents like this have become more frequent in recent years.
  • Wagner is part of the curatorial team behind the exhibition "Never Again!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Young people pose inside a crematorium oven at the Buchenwald concentration camp memorial, laughing while they give the Nazi salute and take pictures of each other. "In a sense, they're trophies to post on social media for them to boast about — breaking the ultimate taboo," Jens-Christian Wagner, director of the Buchenwald and Mittelbau-Dora Memorials Foundation, told DW.

"Incidents like this have become more frequent in recent years. We have seen memorial trees planted in honor of concentration camp victims cut down. When something like this happens — and it happens regularly — I find it particularly despicable because, because it ultimately kills these people a second time," added Wagner.

Wagner is part of the curatorial team behind the exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in Bonn's Bundeskunsthalle, or the Art and Exhibition Hall of the Federal Republic of Germany. Wagner said Holocaust remembrance is under pressure, and the subject of intensifying attacks.

Critics have dismissed remembrance as a "cult of guilt" or "national masochism." With right-wing populism on the rise and historical revisionism becoming more common, Wagner worries about how Germany will remember the victims murdered by the Nazi regime. He is also concerned about the future of democracy. And soon, there will be no Holocaust survivors left to tell the true story of what happened.

This newly introduced exhibition tackles this concern head-on with numerous works of art and historical artifacts.

Recent findings suggest that "I hope that perhaps even some people who don't already believe it's important to confront Nazi crimes will find their way to the exhibition," Wagner mentioned. Memorial sites also attract visitors who aren't necessarily convinced of the need to confront these parts of history. Many of them are students.

"Let's not kid ourselves: When a teacher indicates 'We're going there,' it's always a mandatory visit," he said.

For today's young people, the Nazi era seems like the distant past, Wagner explained. "When you tell them to remember something that their grandparents didn't even experience, it naturally feels like an emotional burden. They can practically see the finger being wagged at them, and that doesn't exactly encourage learning.".

It has been revealed that A two-hour lecture won't have much of an impact if pupils aren't even paying attention. Instead, Buchenwald organizes full-day programs that allow students to explore historical sources together and make sense of history for themselves.

The next step, Wagner mentioned, is to show young people that this chapter of history isn't closed. Visitors are encouraged to make connections between the past and current events like migration, for example.

"For the longest time, people have been discussing migration almost exclusively in terms of threats to public safety and crime. This broadly marginalizes certain groups — a mechanism that also worked for National Socialism," he noted.

Eva Umlauf, 83, knows firsthand what it means to experience exclusion in its most extreme form. She is a patron of the Bonn exhibition.

Recent findings suggest that in November 1944, Umlauf was just 2 years old when she, her pregnant mother and her father were deported by the Nazis from the Novaky labor camp in Slovakia to Auschwitz-Birkenau, the notorious Nazi concentration and extermination camp. She was saved from the gas chambers by mere days; the Nazis stopped using the chambers as the Red Army advanced, hoping to hide evidence of their crimes.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Industry observers note that the camp was liberated on January 27, 1945. Three months later, Umlauf's sister Nora was born. But her father, her mother's siblings and her grandparents were all murdered. Eva barely survived herself. She suffered from tuberculosis, rickets and whooping cough, as well as edema caused by starvation. "Forget about the child. She won't survive," a doctor told her mother. But he was wrong.

It has been revealed that her mother returned to what was then Czechoslovakia with her two daughters, settling in Trencin. Eva Umlauf has no conscious memories of Auschwitz, but she carries her family's trauma deep within her.

Her mother never talked about what happened. Even so, Eva knew from an early age that she was a survivor. Her family rarely mentioned the camp by name, but one sentence came up again and again: "They stayed there." Eva knew that meant "they" were dead. And then, there was the number tattooed onto her arm: A26959.

Industry observers note that her mother taught her daughters not to draw attention to their Jewish identity — antisemitism was widespread throughout Czechoslovakia at the time. The small family managed to avoid harassment.

Industry observers note that eva Umlauf wanted to become a pediatrician, so she studied medicine. In the 1960s, she met her future husband, Jakob, who had also survived the Holocaust. He was an architect, active in Munich's Jewish community. They married in 1966, and she moved to Germany. She could hardly have imagined that she would one day live in the country of the perpetrators. "I don't hate Germans," she said. "But I cannot forgive. How can you forgive the deaths of 6 million people?".

It has been revealed that it wasn't until much later that she first spoke publicly about the horrors of her early childhood. In 2011, she delivered a commemorative speech in Auschwitz on the anniversary of the camp's liberation. Since 2025, she has served as chair of the International Auschwitz Committee. A heart attack in 2014 motivated her to write her first book. "I was in intensive care. I thought to myself: If I get out of here healthy, I'll write a book.".

Recent findings suggest that her memoir, "The Number on Your Forearm is Blue Like Your Eyes," was first released in 2016. The English translation followed in 2024. Since its publication, hardly a day has passed without someone asking Eva Umlauf to share her story.

Recent findings suggest that she is appalled by the disrespectful behavior of young people at former concentration camps and by growing ignorance about the Holocaust. Sometimes, people even ask if she's too old to have a tattoo. But she also recalls a young man on the Munich subway who noticed the number on her arm and told her: "I want to apologize to you for what my ancestors did to you.".

It has been revealed that umlauf never imagined that antisemitism would once again become so widespread in Europe and the United States. Nor did she expect the rise of Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

Recent findings suggest that "I go into schools. I'm so overwhelmed by the number of requests asking for my availability. And yet, the AfD is growing faster than I can reach students. It makes me think all this work is for nothing," she told DW.

Germany must never again fall under a right-wing dictatorship, she stressed. "'Never again' sounds nice, but all I can say is: It's happening again! Wouldn't 'Here We Go Again: Never Again' make a good title for the exhibition?".

It has been revealed that she also shared her message to young people in the exhibition catalog, "Never Again": "You are not responsible for the crimes of your grandparents and great-grandparents. But you are responsible for the future. […] You are the generation that will shape our world. Make it a place where everyone can grow up safely, regardless of their background, faith or skin color.".

She continues: "You don't have to be perfect. You just have to stay alert. Take care of your country.".

The exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in the Bundeskunsthalle in Bonn runs through May 2, 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) firm.
  • The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) firm.

The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.

The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believe she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

US government officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before US President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May.

Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy has exposed him and the company to criticism that it may have allowed China to obtain valuable trade secrets as Beijing tries to gain an edge in the race to develop advanced AI models.

It has been revealed that nvidia is initiating an investigation led by independent board members and an external law firm. It said in a statement that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.".

In a recent development, "The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders," the firm mentioned Sunday. "While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information.".

The organization's shares fell in early trading on Monday.

While US intelligence officials have not commented publicly on the claims, Trump — with whom Jensen Huang has a close relationship — has backed the Nvidia boss.

"He's an honorable guy," said Trump. "I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he's a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on. I hope everything's fine.".

Tim Culpan, an Asia tech reporter who has covered Nvidia and Huang closely for years, told DW that while Nvidia's fundamental strengths as a tech giant remain in place, Huang is hugely personally damaged by the story.

"They're still going to make great chips and they're going to sell them to millions of customers around the world who want the best AI chips in the world," he said.

In a recent development, "His opinion is going to carry a lot less weight now. And that, in the long term, will flow through to Nvidia and Nvidia's own corporate interests. So it won't be immediate. It's really a fact that he doesn't have the sway or the power that he might have had one week ago simply through this.".

Richard Windsor, a tech analyst and the founder of research tech giant Radio Free Mobile, said the news could be very serious for Nvidia given how much the company has revolved around Huang for decades.

"This problem is particularly acute because Jensen Huang is very hands-on, meaning that the key decisions that led to its success were ultimately taken by him and because there is no obvious successor," he mentioned.

"I suspect we are about to find out just how much the market thinks that the firm is dependent on its iconic founder and CEO.".

Nvidia and Huang's attitude toward China and potential Chinese customers has been a bone of contention with US intelligence officials — despite Huang's close relationship with Trump.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to ease restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China. A 2025 export control deal heavily curbed sales, but Trump subsequently permitted the export of older H200 Nvidia chips to China in return for the US government receiving a cut of the sales.

However, that deal has been complicated and bogged down by Washington's strict export-license review. China has also initiated import controls, despite strong demand from Chinese companies. China lacks access to the most advanced AI-capable chips. Beijing wants to develop its own alternatives but has struggled to catch up.

Huang has argued that Chinese dependence on Nvidia's chips would prevent rivals such as Huawei from catching up and boosting China's ambitions to dominate AI supply chains.

Industry observers note that however, that argument has been dismissed by many US intelligence officials. They fear that unlimited Chinese access to the most advanced Nvidia chips would boost China's domestic AI sector, lead to its AI models catching up with the leading US models and see the chips being used in Chinese military applications.

Industry observers note that the US-China rivalry has become a central theme in the global AI story, with both countries seeking to gain an upper hand in the technology. Leading US AI executives such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei have argued that US AI companies can't afford to take a prolonged pause to allow safety standards in AI to catch up, if they're going to prevent Chinese firms from gaining an advantage.

Washington's central fear over Huang's affair is that it could have led to Beijing obtaining vital trade secrets or other key information about how Nvidia makes its most advanced chips.

It has been revealed that windsor thinks Huang will survive the "severe test" due to his importance to the organization. He also cast doubt on the extent to which Beijing and its leading tech firms have learned from Nvidia's chips, pointing to China's own chip ambitions and commitment to have its firms buy its own semiconductors.

"I am far from convinced that Chinese AI has materially benefited from technology or illicit chip imports that it gained from Nvidia," he remarked.

The news comes at a particularly challenging moment for Nvidia, which has benefited massively from the AI boom thanks to its position as the leading maker of cutting-edge semiconductors needed for AI applications.

Nvidia's valuation has soared dramatically in recent years as companies rushed to buy its chips, becoming the world's first $5 trillion organization in October 2025.

Industry observers note that however, doubts over the sustainability of the $9 trillion capital expenditure AI boom have sparked a major sell-off in stocks related to the boom in recent weeks. The Democrats' sweeping victories in the US midterms have added to the doubts, given the strength of voter opposition to data center construction in the US.

It has been revealed that in the city that saw them lift the Europa League in May, Villa produced a limp display against a Galatasaray side missing star centre-forward Victor Osimhen. Villa failed to register a shot on target and are now without a win in six games in all competitions.

Substitute Deniz Gul headed the only goal 13 minutes from time as Villa boss Unai Emery cut an angry figure on the touchline and was booked late on. He also appeared to have a tense exchange with midfielder Ross Barkley.

Here Daily Mail Sport's TOM COLLOMOSSE looks at the key moments from another unconvincing Villa display.

Aston Villa left John McGinn out of the starting XI last Saturday and dropped two points in a drab 0-0 draw with Sunderland.

Industry observers note that the skipper was back here but three minutes after he was taken off, Villa conceded. Careless defending at a corner allowed Gul to head home, though he took an accidental boot in the face from Nicolas Jackson that required lengthy treatment.

Unai Emery's decision to substitute John McGinn backfired as Aston Villa lost at Galatasaray.

Villa conceded three minutes after Emery decided to take off his captain (left) in Istanbul.

Deniz Gul scored the only goal of the game with a close-range header on Tuesday evening.

Aston Villa (4-2-3-1): Suzuki 6; Harwood-Bellis 6, Lindelof 7, Mings 6, Maatsen 5; Kamara 7 (Buendia 82), J Gomes 6 (Goretzka 66, 6); Alysson 5 (Mbaye 66, 5), McGinn 7 (Barkley 74, 6), Manzambi 5 (Hemmings 74, 6); Jackson 5.

Booked: Jackson, McGinn, J Gomes, Emery.

In a recent development, during one clash in the first half with Gala defender Davinson Sanchez, Villa boss Unai Emery raced to the edge of his technical area to stop Jackson talking his way into the book. Emery succeeded that time, but not long afterwards, Jackson was punished for a needless tussle with Wilfried Singo.

In a recent development, jackson plays on the edge. That is a substantial part of his game. He is also 26 next June and has enough experience to understand when to step into an argument and when to hold back. Emery does not count on Tammy Abraham much these days and Brian Madjo is raw, so he needs Jackson to keep his cool.

Recent findings suggest that the Senegal forward was not the only one to test the patience of referee Daniel Siebert. Joao Gomes was lucky only to be booked for bringing down Yunus Akgun and then grabbing his opponent, while John McGinn was furious that Aleksey Batrakov escaped with a booking for appearing to kick out at the Villa skipper.

Nicolas Jackson's ill-discipline is a concern, with the striker having collected four yellow cards.

For most of the last four years, any Villa fan could have written down Emery's first choice XI. Not these days, as Emery still seems to be searching for the ideal formula.

His uncertainty is understandable after losing five key outfield players in the summer but Villa's fortunes this season may depend on how swiftly Emery can make up his mind.

37 years after fall of Berlin Wall: How divided are Germans?

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1363 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when the Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, ending East Germany's isolation from the West, the event was celebrated on both sides of the border.
  • Surveys show that only a minority of respondents report feeling a strong sense of community between those from former East and West Germany, and many continue to perceive significant differences.
  • To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when the Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, ending East Germany's isolation from the West, the event was celebrated on both sides of the border. Yet, 37 years later, many people on both sides remain deeply skeptical of each other.

Surveys show that only a minority of respondents report feeling a strong sense of community between those from former East and West Germany, and many continue to perceive significant differences.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

We asked three artists from Germany with different perspectives on the history of the country's division to share their views.

Author Lea Streisand was born in 1979 and experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall firsthand while growing up in East Berlin.

In her books and essays, she has returned to her East German upbringing many times, using literature to process it.

The novel "Hufeland, at the corner of Bötzow" (2019, Ullstein), for example, recounts the period of reunification from a child's perspective.

"November 9, 1989, was simply incredible," she told DW. She was 10 years old at the time. When her mother bought her winter boots with the 100 Deutsche Marks she received from the West German state — a welcome gift given to all East German citizens — she was so disappointed that she felt like crying. But later, a friend of her parents' let her buy so many sweets at the supermarket that they lasted until Christmas.

"The disappointment really set in afterwards, with what happened over the course of the following year. It was unbelievable how quickly an entire system was suddenly swept away and a latest one built up, as if to say, 'There you go. You're welcome'," Streisand recalled. "I think it was just too fast for people.".

Recent findings suggest that the people of East Germany, or the GDR, had brought about the fall of the Berlin Wall themselves through a civil rights movement and numerous demonstrations. For many, however, the goal was not to dissolve the state immediately but to reform it.

Recent findings suggest that among them was Anke Feuchtenberger, born in 1963 in East Berlin. Her childhood was spent in East Berlin and in the East German region of Western Pomerania, where she now lives again and feels "very much at home.".

In a recent development, today, she teaches at the University of Applied Sciences in Hamburg, meaning she spends time on both sides of the former divide. Feuchtenberger is often described as Germany's most influential comic artist. Her work has also garnered international acclaim.

"Back then, as artists, we tried to bring about a change through posters and flyers — to gain more freedom without immediately abolishing socialism," she explained.

It has been revealed that at the time, the fall of the Berlin Wall stirred up mixed feelings in Feuchtenberger: "I soon realized that the creative and revolutionary aspects of our movement were very quickly being smothered by consumerism, and that nationalist tendencies — which had already been noticeable before — were coming to the fore," Feuchtenberger recalled. "That made me afraid.".

Meanwhile, for photographic artist Simon Menner, born in 1978 in Emmendingen, in the West German state of Baden-Württemberg, Berlin was very far away. As Menner put it, he experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall as a child in a "rather abstract" way. Today, Berlin is his home.

Industry observers note that in his experience, the way films and documentaries portrayed East Germany around the time of reunification was very bleak. "But West Germany in the '80s," he said, "was also bleak and very staid.".

This uneven portrayal of the two parts of Germany is an problem that deeply concerns Menner — partly because he unwittingly contributed to it in a small way. Among other things, Menner's work explores the topic of surveillance and how it works.

In the archives of East Germany's Ministry for State Security, or Stasi — which are freely accessible today as part of the National Archives — he discovered a massive collection of photographs that both fascinated and horrified him and which he wanted to bring to the attention of a wider public.

Sources indicate that his photo book "Top Secret" (2012, from publisher Hatje Cantz) features a selection of photos that offer a unique insight into the work of the Stasi. Some are eerie, while others are curious or even absurd.

According to recent reports, menner also tried to look into the photo archive of West Germany's Federal Intelligence Service. "I spent a year trying to gain access — without success," he remarked.

In hindsight, he now finds his artistic project problematic because he believes it is too one-sided, focusing exclusively on East Germany's past.

It has been revealed that according to Menner, West Germany's intelligence services in the 1960s were not exactly models of virtue either, and he believes it is "actually high time" to critically examine this part of history as well. In his view, an honest examination of Germany's past as a whole is a prerequisite for genuine reconciliation.

Recent findings suggest that streisand believes literature can help foster mutual understanding. "Literature opens a window into experiences we haven't had ourselves," she said. "You can immerse yourself in the mind of someone who has had a different life than you have and understand what happened.".

Recent findings suggest that interest in these stories remains strong. In 2023, Feuchtenberger published the nearly 500-page graphic novel "Comrade Cuckoo" (published by Reprodukt), which was the first graphic novel to be nominated for the Leipzig Book Fair Prize in the fiction category.

It has been revealed that the story spans a childhood in the fictional East German village of Pritschitanow in the 1960s in the GDR to the post-Reunification era. In it, Feuchtenberger weaves autobiographical memories of her upbringing with fantastical and fictional elements.

The artist remarked she was surprised "that, so long after the fall of the wall, my stories have sparked such great interest in the West.".

In particular, the fact that the main character, Kerstin, rarely sees her parents because they both work full-time is a topic that often comes up at readings. In the GDR, everyone had the right to work, she noted. At the same time, it was a civic duty.

Could the West German interest in this stem from the fact that full-time employment for both parents has long been less common in the West? It's possible, said Feuchtenberger.

When looking toward their shared future, the two East German women are more optimistic than Menner, from West Germany.

"In Berlin, I often don't even notice anymore whether I'm in the West or the East," said Menner. "But when it comes to sociopolitical concerns, politicians should listen to older and younger people more closely," he added, referring to the recent election successes of far-right Alternative for Germany, or AfD . "Otherwise, things are going to get difficult in the near future.".

"It's very notable to step outside our own bubble because people all over the world are facing problems. Constantly focusing on this German-German divide that has emerged between the groups doesn't help," said Feuchtenberger.

"For me personally, the whole glitch of borders has somehow dissolved," she explained. This is due in no small part to the many trips abroad that have taken her to various places around the world.

Moreover, in her hometown near the Polish border, she observes how animals couldn't care less about the border. "They come from the east and the west and do whatever they want," she remarked. That's why she also gave "Comrade Cuckoo" the working title "A German Animal in a German Forest," "because I found the absurdity of an animal having a nationality so funny.".

According to recent reports, "This East-West thing — our children won't have any interest in it at all," stated Streisand. "Young people don't care where their parents come from. Can I get a job that will support a family? Do I have to go to war? Right now, completely different things are relevant.".

It has been revealed that this Brighton and Hove Albion title challenge – as it must now be classed – flies in the face of the saying that money always talks in football. Manchester City have been found guilty of breaching financial rules and also fielded the most expensive midfield in Premier League history here, yet the match-winners cost a fraction in comparison.

Looking at Brighton’s winning goal, it was created by a cross that flashed across the City goal from Diego Gómez, an £11m signing who was playing in Major League Soccer in the United States not so long ago. Maxim de Cuyper, a £17.5m arrival from Club Brugge, was credited with the assist after Yasin Ayari tapped in.

According to recent reports, ayari cost £3.5m from Swedish club AIK and scored in the 5-0 wins over Coventry and Palace, and now has this winner to add to his collection. The 23-year-old is another example of Brighton polishing these gems and putting them together in a team that can win against any opponent in the Premier League.

It could keep them at the top end of the table for a good while longer. They have already shown they can defeat Arsenal in a one-off match and they look to have the ingredients to stay the pace with them. In Fabian Hürzeler they have one of the brightest young coaches in the Premier League and he has a squad that are all on the same page.

Recent findings suggest that leicester upset the odds 10 years ago with a settled team, while this Brighton team has a deeper squad. When the substitutes came on in the second half, they slotted into a well-rehearsed system.

“We faced adversity. There was a little bit of luck but in the end they deserved it because they worked hard for it,” said Hürzeler. “I want players who want to compete, to dominate. “Unfortunately it is happening for our players but I think it is part of the game, part of football, it happens many times against us, we need to analyse and understand what we can do better,” Maresca added. City also felt Dunk used his arm to block the ball in the penalty area, although no spot-kick was given.

Sources indicate that it was a sweet goal by Ayari, who had missed a penalty in the shoot-out last week when the teams played in the EFL Cup. Brighton stayed in Manchester after the defeat, masterminding a win that means they have now defeated all of the traditional heavyweight teams in the Premier League.

“I wasn’t aware of that. For me it’s more key, not about history, it’s about giving something back to the supporters. They’ve spent a lot of time and money,” Hürzeler mentioned.

“We’ll take it game by game. See what happens because we have loads of games. Just focussing every day on what’s ahead of us and the job we have. We will continue to do that and see where it leaves us at the end of the season. We are happy with the way we are playing - not just the results but the way we are playing too. We have to continue to develop that style and ruthlessness and we can do great things.”.

In City-related matters, Jack Grealish is battling for his future next season and faces becoming the Premier League’s most high-profile free agent following his breach of discipline at Everton.

The 31-year-old, who became the first £100m signing by an English club in 2021, is out of contract in eight months and his hopes of staying on Merseyside took a hit when the club decided he would not play in the Carabao Cup win over Newcastle.

While City head coach Enzo Maresca described Grealish as “a good boy with a major heart”, there are no signs of him getting a contract extension at the Etihad Stadium after being loaned out in the last two seasons.

“It is not correct to talk about Jack as he is an Everton player and I don’t have all the information,” stated Maresca, who worked with Grealish when he was in Pep Guardiola’s backroom staff. “I still think he is a good guy, a good boy with a massive heart.”.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Saturday’s 3pm Premier League kick-offs.

The most eye-catching fixture sees Manchester City host Brighton & Hove Albion for the second time this week at the Etihad Stadium. On Wednesday evening in the League Cup, Enzo Maresca’s side squeezed past Fabian Hurzeler’s men on penalties (4-3) thanks to second-choice goalkeeper Geronimo Rulli’s heroics after drawing 2-2 in normal time.
