Tech Report: Buy-Back Clauses in Football: Everything You Need to Know

📅 24 Jul 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (772 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Givemesport

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amid all the focus on FFP and PSR, especially in the Premier League, clubs are trying to find more ways to find value for money and also insure themselves for the future - something perhaps most clearly seen in the form of buy-back clauses.
  • A key feature in the early stages of the window has been clubs inserting buy-back clauses in deals for departing players.
  • If a player develops better than the selling club had first thought, they would then feel they could bring them back at a transfer fee below their now increased market value.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amid all the focus on FFP and PSR, especially in the Premier League, clubs are trying to find more ways to find value for money and also insure themselves for the future - something perhaps most clearly seen in the form of buy-back clauses.

A key feature in the early stages of the window has been clubs inserting buy-back clauses in deals for departing players. This allows established clubs to let talented young players leave, with the insurance policy that if they succeed, they have the option to bring them back for a price already determined at the point of the original sale.

If a player develops better than the selling club had first thought, they would then feel they could bring them back at a transfer fee below their now increased market value. Additionally, if a rival reveals interest, they would have the option to sign them at a price lower than what the current club might demand of other teams.

Sources indicate that real Madrid have regularly used buy-back clauses since the early 2010s, with examples including Alvaro Morata, Lucas Vazquez, Dani Carvajal and Casemiro. Carvajal was sold to Bayer Leverkusen for approximately €5 million in July 2012, with a buy-back option for Madrid to resign the player for €6.5 million after one year and €7 million after two years.

The Spanish right-back impressed in the Bundesliga and was resigned by Madrid the following summer. Since then, he has won the Champions League six times with the club.

They used the buy-back clause differently when they exercised the option to resign Morata in 2016. After only a season at Madrid in his second spell for the club, the Spanish striker was sold for £60 million to Chelsea. The 15-time Champions League winners resigned Morata for around £26 million, meaning they made a hefty profit on the 31-year-old.

Industry observers note that los Blancos' buyback clause tactic was also used when Nico Paz left for Como 1907 in 2024. They inserted an €80m clause into the deal and he has swiftly become one of the most skillful players in the world.

Dani Carvajal's Real Madrid career.

Industry observers note that the first high-profile example of a buy-back clause being used in English football was back in 1983. Luther Blissett was involved in this deal, as he was sold from Watford to AC Milan for £1 million. After an unsuccessful year in Italy, the Hertfordshire club exercised a clause in his contract that gave them first refusal on Blissett. As a result, Watford resigned the striker for £550,000 a year later.

In a recent development, in recent times, clubs have let their stars go without exercising the buy-back option. Tammy Abraham is a prime example of this, as he was sold to Roma from Chelsea for £34 million in 2021. The Blues had a buy-back clause of around £68 million, but never triggered it during his time in Italy.

Douglas Luiz was also signed by Aston Villa from Manchester City in 2019 for a fee of around £15 million. A buy-back option that expired in June 2021 was included.

However, City did not exercise this option and the Brazilian went on to become a well-established member of Unai Emery's side, before leaving the club in 2024.

Sometimes, it's simply worth including a buy-back clause just in case. It is better to be safe than sorry, especially in today's market. Clubs don't always heed that warning, though, and many have been left to live with their transfer regret as a result. Man City instantly stand out as a fine example.

The Citizens sold Cole Palmer to Chelsea for just £40m in 2023. At the time, he was nothing more than untapped potential which had been left sealed shut by a lack of opportunities at Man City. Everyone at the Etihad knew that the potential was, nonetheless, there in abundance, however. All Palmer needed was the opportunity, and Chelsea gave him just that.

The England international has become a world-beater at Stamford Bridge. Chelsea have unleashed that untapped potential. Man City, meanwhile, have been forced to watch on after deciding against inserting a buy-back clause into their 2024 sale.

Recent findings suggest that it's not just Man City who have been forced to live with their regret, though. Chelsea, themselves, instantly regretted their decision not to include a buy-back clause when they sold Kevin De Bruyne to Wolfsburg in 2014. He went onto become one of the best midfielders in Premier League history after completing a major money move to Man City just 18 months later.

#118131. Industry News: AI in classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1407 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: AI in classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1407 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium.
  • "I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW.
  • Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium. He and his classmates have already been using artificial intelligence-enabled tools, or AI, for the last two and a half years.

"I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW. Jakob isn't his real name, because he doesn't want to publicly admit he and many others of his age use AI to do their homework.

Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.

In science, this is called "cognitive outsourcing." Basically, the required thinking is shifted to another device, whether that's a calculator, notepad or a large language model (LLM) like ChatGPT.

There's a difference with AI, though. A notepad or calculator can take over a step or two but rarely the whole thought process. That's not the same for an LLM, which can handle the entire problem-solving process.

It has been revealed that jakob admitted he's also had an AI help him with his homework. "But only when I was really stuck," he insisted. And he's also aware that it can become a problem when AI does all your homework. "The students who get good grades tend not to do that," he explained.

Franziska Müller has been a German teacher for several decades and is presently teaching senior classes at a gymnasium. Her name has also been changed for privacy reasons.

"They can't even think for themselves anymore," she told DW, complaining about some of her classes.

Industry observers note that even in ordinary classes, some of the students type their questions into their tablets or phones, asking for AI assistance. And should they be called upon in class, she knows that they're reading out the answers that the AI has prepared for them and hoping nobody notices.

Müller believes students these days are less able to comprehend text. "Because they read less and let AI summarize almost everything for them," she remarked.

Several studies have reached very similar conclusions.

That includes the latest PISA (Program for International Student Assessment) study from September. PISA, which is run by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, regularly evaluates the abilities of 15-year-old students around the world.

It has been revealed that "Students who report using AI chatbots get lower scores in science, on average, than those who don't use AI," Andreas Schleicher, the OECD director for education and skills, wrote in his report in October. "This includes using AI to summarize texts they had to read, conduct preliminary research on a latest topic, or draft texts for writing assignments.".

Sources indicate that with participants from more than 90 countries, PISA is considered the largest international comparative study of 15-year-olds worldwide. This year, German 15-year-olds posted their lowest PISA scores in the 25-year history of the study.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"The connections are complex and depend heavily on how generative AI is used, but the central insight is simple: Just as we don't get fit by watching sports but by doing sports ourselves, learning doesn't come from consuming content, but from the mind's productive cognitive engagement with new material," Schleicher explained.

Put simply, those who don't exercise their brains risk becoming less intelligent.

US think tank, the Brookings Institution, has already argued that the risks of using AI in education outweigh the benefits.

Its own research, which included young participants from around the world, speaks of students losing "fundamental cognitive and durable skills as they increasingly rely on AI to perform learning's intellectual work," as well as the decline of critical thinking, memory, perseverance and independent judgment.

But what can be done against the power of ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini and Meta AI?

Fresh York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has banned the use of AI in public schools up to the eighth grade for the 2026 and 2027 school years — so that's up to about the age of 14 or 15.

Not everyone agrees this is the right thing to do. Julian Hinn, who teaches German to students aged between 15 and 18 in Germany, said class members can still use AI apps on their mobile phones. "And anyone who thinks they won't use it at home is ignoring reality," Hinn told DW.

Germany's annual JIM study, which tracks teenagers' media use and device ownership, supports that view.

91% of young people surveyed in Germany, between the ages of 12 and 19, stated that they use at least one AI application. The study also reports that 74% use AI for homework and learning.

It has been revealed that the last JIM study actually dates back to 2024 so those percentages might be even higher now. Data on AI use in Asia, Latin America and the US from the Brookings study show similarly high figures.

German politicians have recognized the problem. Although education in Germany is the responsibility of the individual federal states, the so-called Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, or KMK, has been issuing statements on the use of AI since 2024.

The KMK's statements have been rather vague though, saying only that students should be enabled to engage with AI in a critical, reflective and responsible manner.

Teachers and students alike are aware that AI can be a powerful support in the classroom.

"The AIs simply explain things much better than textbooks," stated Jakob, adding that he'll often get an AI to explain basic concepts to him.

Sometimes teachers can't respond like an AI, Hinn conceded. "The AI ​​can respond much better to the language and needs of the students.".

According to recent reports, that's why he thinks it's important to include AI in classes, starting from the 10th grade when students are around 15 or 16. Hinn doesn't think it should be introduced before that, when children's basic skills are still being developed.

Recent findings suggest that in more senior classes, Hinn will encourage his students to question the AI critically. "We look at the quality of the solutions," he explained.

German teacher Müller has also integrated some use of AI into her lessons for older students. But in some aspects of the class, she also bans it altogether so that her students can focus on thinking for themselves.

"I understand very well that it's tempting to use AI," she mentioned.

According to recent reports, there are also other problems with AI in education. According to the Brookings study, students with basic skills can use AI to deepen their learning and progress faster.

But for children with gaps in their knowledge, they tend to adopt AI's errors, outsource their thinking and then fall even further behind. In this way, AI can exacerbate preexisting inequalities.

The PISA study notes that children from more affluent backgrounds often have a better start, and AI can widen that gap.

This is called the Matthew effect — the name comes from the biblical verse Matthew 25:29, "for unto everyone that hath shall be given." It basically means that early success in learning leads to better progress in the future, while early struggles equal a growing lag over time.

In the age of AI, teachers have become more motivated to challenge students to think independently and to consider their own personal autonomy.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Hinn, who also supervises the school newspaper, said: "I always tell everyone, you can use AI but the feeling of having written an article with your own pen is spectacular.".

Industry observers note that both teachers also stress the idea of personal autonomy and responsibility. They believe this affects the students, especially because when they sit exams, they aren't allowed to use any aids or AI. And if they aren't able to solve their own problems, they will fail.

It's during exam time that the students really find out if they can solve those math, English or science problems by themselves.

Müller mentioned one of her students recently confessed they were upset after a poor exam result. "He felt he simply couldn't think for himself anymore because of AI," she said.

This article was originally written in German.

#118129. Latest Update: ‘The worst COP ever’ offers a chance to learn from failure

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1199 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: ‘The worst COP ever’ offers a chance to learn from failure

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1199 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, protesters on the final day of the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey.
  • ‘The worst COP ever’ is how some people have described the United Nations COP31 climate meeting in Antalya, Turkey, which ended on 22 November.
  • The world’s first plastics treaty is in crisis: can it be salvaged?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, protesters on the final day of the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey. Credit: Chris McGrath/Getty.

‘The worst COP ever’ is how some people have described the United Nations COP31 climate meeting in Antalya, Turkey, which ended on 22 November. COP31 was the first to take place after the confirmation that global warming will overshoot the safe limit of 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels. Despite a two-day extension to the meeting and several proposals for an overarching political declaration or ‘cover decision’, delegates left after two weeks of talks without such an agreement.

The world’s first plastics treaty is in crisis: can it be salvaged?

The world’s first plastics treaty is in crisis: can it be salvaged?

Drafted by the host nations (Turkey and Australia, this year), a cover decision is a statement that all countries can agree on at the end of the talks. It is not a legally binding text and is a relatively recent innovation. That participants failed to agree such a statement is not a surprise. It requires a willingness for give and take, which was in short supply because many of the countries that attended this year are at war, subject to economic and other sanctions, or involved in trade disputes. Furthermore, the United States, the world’s biggest economy and the largest historic carbon emitter, did not attend following its withdrawal from the COP process.

Industry observers note that delegates from the world’s poorest countries were angry that there was no mention of concrete measures to increase finance for climate adaptation — money that they will need to help them to become more resilient to climate shocks. Many delegates were also angry that the draft text did not include any reference to transitioning away from fossil fuels. Previous cover decisions have included such language, overcoming objections from fossil-fuel-producing states. This time, however, delegates from these states were more determined to block such wording.

It has been revealed that but there are key reasons why it would be wrong to conclude that such climate conferences have outlived their purpose — or that a consensus-based approach should be abandoned, as some have argued. There is always room to improve, but COP meetings are much more than what happens in the final days when high-level political representatives turn up.

Environmental treaties are paralysed — here’s how we can do better.

Environmental treaties are paralysed — here’s how we can do better.

First, these meetings mainly involve discussions between technical experts and observers — including many researchers — representing the countries that have signed up to the UN’s climate agreement, known as the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. For most of the two weeks (and in many timetabled talks before a COP), delegates meet in working groups to discuss a spectrum of climate-change topics. The Antalya meeting discussions included how to accelerate electrification, cut methane emissions and mobilize upcoming finance to protect the world’s forests. Progress in these technical talks is often incremental. In contrast to the final days of a COP, which are organized around negotiations between political representatives, expert delegates focus on getting things done rather than posturing.

The second reason not to write off this COP is that it’s not uncommon for countries to leave meetings without a high-level agreement. Indeed, some previous ‘good’ outcomes needed earlier COP meetings to ‘fail’. The landmark COP21 Paris climate agreement signed in 2015, a legally binding text in which nations agreed to limit global warming to 1.5 °C, is perhaps the best-known example. In 2009, COP15 in Copenhagen resulted in deadlock. That failure prompted deeper thinking and discussions at subsequent COP meetings on the steps needed for the world to stay within safe climate limits, laying the groundwork for the Paris agreement.

Industry observers note that still, the current geopolitical climate is a substantial obstacle to progress, affecting not only COP climate meetings but also talks on other international agreements, such as a proposed treaty to end plastic pollution. Another set of talks occurring at the same time as COP31 — on setting international restrictions on autonomous weapons — also failed to reach an agreement and will resume in 2028.

In the case of both the climate and plastics talks, a relatively small group of countries — including Iran, Russia and Saudi Arabia, which are heavily reliant on fossil-fuel exports, among others — are blocking stronger action. Some researchers, as well as country delegates, say that the UN’s method of decision-making (that all countries must agree a consensus) is the problem, and question whether there should instead be a vote and a decision made by majority.

Trust and science: the essential elements missing from plastics treaty talks.

Trust and science: the essential elements missing from plastics treaty talks.

According to recent reports, there is some logic in changing the approach for the cover decisions to avoid the overtly self-interested blocking of action. But for many other decisions made at UN climate and other environment-related meetings, abandoning a consensus-based approach in favour of a vote would not be a good option.

The UN’s expert groups for example, including the scientists who are part of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (which synthesizes studies to inform decisions), must continue to work through consensus. Delegates painstakingly review, debate and discuss evidence, before coming to a conclusion — and it is important that all those involved are brought in at this point.

A change to voting might, in some cases, mean faster results, but it would also undermine the principles that everyone owns the result and that global problems need global solutions.

Recent findings suggest that it is right that, on reflecting on the COP in Antalya, many will ask what needs to change. And some aspects must. But altering how decisions are made should not be taken lightly. Climate change doesn’t respect borders. It won’t be solved by countries working on their own or in small groups.

It has been revealed that tenerife won 5-2 at Badajoz in the Copa del Rey despite finishing the match with ten men. The victory keeps their cup run alive ahead of the second-round draw.

According to recent reports, at the Estadio Nuevo Vivero on Wednesday 18 November, Álvaro Cervera’s side booked a place in the second round of the Copa del Rey. The tie had been postponed twice, first after the train accident in Toledo province and then after the death of Tenerife forward Jesús de Miguel on 3 November, who was remembered with a minute’s silence.

Cervera started a line-up made up largely of reserves. It still produced a scoreline Tenerife had never recorded in 260 Copa del Rey matches, according to elDiario.es (Canarias Ahora). About 3,000 spectators watched, around 20 per cent of the stadium’s capacity.

Grant-Leon Ranos opened the scoring in the sixth minute from a Marc Mateu assist. Juanjo Sánchez added a second a minute later. Ranos struck again in the 38th minute, set up by Gerard Valentín.

Carlos Beitia pulled one back for Badajoz in the 49th minute. Roko Jureškin was then sent off in the 58th minute. Ten-man Tenerife still extended the lead through substitute Iván Chapela in the 69th minute, assisted by Martin Pečar.

According to recent reports, jorge Barba replied for the hosts in the 74th minute from a Manuel Hernández assist. Víctor Moreno completed the scoring deep into stoppage time, with Álvarez providing the pass.

In a recent development, the Segunda Federación side went into the tie third in their group. They were also unbeaten in seven league matches in a row.

In a recent development, tenerife have now come through their opening Copa del Rey tie in eight seasons in a row. The win followed a 2-0 victory over AD Ceuta FC. Before that came a run of draws against FC Andorra, Sabadell, Celta de Vigo II and Girona.

Industry observers note that this was the first meeting between the clubs in the cup. They had played each other 22 times in Segunda División. Tenerife won ten of those games, Badajoz eight, and four ended level. Tenerife’s previous visit to Badajoz, on 30 March 2003, ended in a 2-1 defeat under David Amaral.

It's been a terrible few days for Alejandro Garnacho's career and, after Unai Emery was criticised for his comments explaining why he snubbed the winger from Aston Villa's Champions League squad this week, Chelsea owner Behdad Eghbali has twisted the knife further by revealing the baffling reason the club signed the Argentine ahead of last season.

The 22-year-old made just 24 appearances during the 2025/26 season after forcing a move away from Manchester United, having overzealously felt he had outgrown the Red Devils.

He was subsequently sent out on loan to Villa for the current campaign - a decision by the Midlands club's hierarchy that made little sense given their previous issues with the Jadon Sancho and Harvey Elliott loan deals.

Industry observers note that emery effectively dismissed Garnacho by suggesting he wasn't good enough. Recent findings suggest that simon Jordan, a pundit for TalkSport, revealed that he asked Behdad Eghbali why Chelsea signed Garnacho in the first place, despite the ominous red flags. His response was 'It was only £50 million', while he later revealed: "We interviewed him on Zoom.".

It has been revealed that his comments seemed to prove that the Blues' recruitment team didn't do much research before signing him, and it has left plenty of the Stamford Bridge faithful rightfully annoyed. One X user wrote: "‘[Roman] Abramovich sold the club to pure morons," as a second added: "Oh my gosh this is embarrassing." Meanwhile, a third remarked:.

"These are the people running our football club..".

"That's a disgrace to put it in this way," a fourth concluded, as the Blues also signed Jamie Gittens - who has failed to make a Premier League appearance under Xabi Alonso - as well as Jorrel Hato, Mamadou Sarr, Liam Delap, and Dario Essugo in the same summer.

Joao Pedro and Estevao are arguably the only two signings in the same period that worked out. But even then, the latter has struggled for fitness and presently doesn't look poised to reach his full potential.

The sudden increase in attention on Garnacho this week has since made him remove all mention of Aston Villa on his Instagram page - which some outlets are reporting as a 'subtle dig' at the club.

But his social media actions should paint a better picture of just how he is feeling right now as his career takes a massive pause. It should also shine a harsh light on both Villa and Chelsea's poor transfer business, as they continue to sign players their managers have no intention of giving a proper chance.

Bukayo Saka has once again shown why he is one of English footballâs most admired figures, taking time out to donate over a thousand school uniforms to families struggling with the cost of living crisis.

Hailing from Ealing, Saka gifted the uniforms to four local schools, including Greenford High, where he studied as a youngster.

The Arsenal and England winger visited the school personally to surprise pupils, posing for photos, signing autographs, and helping distribute the uniforms to those in need.

Recent findings suggest that sharing images of the day on Instagram, Saka wrote: "Special day going back home to launch our school uniform project. Thank you to all the schools, our partners and everybody else who helped us give to the students.".

In 2022, Saka was awarded the Freedom of the Borough of Ealing in recognition of his sporting achievements and his positive influence on young people, following his standout performances at UEFA Euro 2020.

Meanwhile, Outside Greenford High stands a striking mural of Saka, painted in 2021 at the suggestion of a student, celebrating his rise from local schoolboy to football star.

Sources indicate that city, who seemed in rude health after seven successive wins at the start of the Premier League campaign despite the guilty verdicts in the Premier League’s case against them for financial cheating, have wobbled since then, losing their last two league games. Marc Guéhi and Gigi Donnarumma are both suffering bouts of poor form, other individual errors continue to plague them and, although they are creating hatfuls of chances, they have been thwarted by a combination of imprecise finishing and the excellence of Zion Suzuki and Bart Verbruggen.

Sources indicate that for all their travails on the road – RB Leipzig have also lost at Werder Bremen, Bayer Leverkusen and Bayern Munich – they have won all their home Bundesliga matches as well as a 1-0 victory over PSV in this competition. Their total of 22 league goals is second only to Bayern’s 27 and Antonio Nusa, a Norway team-mate of Erling Haaland, is in sparkling form flitting behind strikers Christopher Nkunku and Romulo. City, whose full-backs, if you can describe the centre-backs and midfielders who play either side of the centre-halves in that way, never look fit for purpose defensively and may well have their work cut out tonight if he drifts wide.

Industry observers note that the Red Bull coaching principles, which have treated us to the dross football of Jesse Marsch, Matthias Jaissle and Ralph Hasenhüttl, all about the long pass, the central channel, counter-pressing and second balls, have a newly introduced proponent in Martín Demichelis, the forner City and Argentina defender who won the title in 2014 at the Etihad. Three years ago he led River Plate to the title in Argentina, the highlight of a coaching career also spent running Bayern’s U21s, Monterey and Mallorca.

These two have met six times in the last five years, City winning four, most notably the 7-0 thrashing at the Etihad in 2023’s Round of 16, the year they went on to win the Treble. Leipzig’s only victory came at home five years ago in the sixth, redundant group game when City and PSG had already clinched qualification for the knockout stages.

Antoine Semenyo is City’s only absentee; Leipzig will have to do without one-cap Germany midfielder Assan Ouédraogo and former Chelsea striker Marc Guiu.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Real Madrid have extended the contracts of Aurélien Tchouaméni and Arda Güler until June 2032, a day apart. With captain Fede Valverde also reportedly agreeing upcoming terms, the club are securing their core midfield for years to come.

It has been revealed that real Madrid have committed two midfield regulars to long-term deals in the space of 24 hours. Güler’s announcement came first, and Aurélien Tchouaméni’s followed.

According to recent reports, both players are part of the core of Mourinho’s midfield. The renewals keep them at the club for six more seasons.

Tchouaméni arrived in 2022 and has made 205 appearances for the club. He has won eight trophies in that time. They include one Champions League, two Club World Cups and two UEFA Super Cups. He has also lifted one LaLiga, one Copa del Rey and one Spanish Super Cup.

Industry observers note that his standing goes beyond the club. He has 50 France caps and won the 2021 Nations League. The latest contract is worth around €9 million net per season, GOAL reported. The agreement came after interest from Manchester United.

In a recent development, güler’s record covers a shorter spell. He was 18 when he joined. He has 38 caps for Turkey. In September he was named Breakthrough Player of the 2025-26 Champions League. His latest salary is reportedly about €8m a year.

Industry observers note that the two profiles differ. Tchouaméni is an established international with a full set of club honours. Güler is a younger player whose contract now runs almost nine years from his arrival. Tying both to the same end date suggests a midfield the club intend to keep together.

Sources indicate that the club may not be finished. Captain Fede Valverde has agreed to extend his contract from 2029 to 2031, according to GOAL. The upcoming deal will make him one of the squad’s highest earners. An announcement is expected soon, as Madrid work on further renewals after Güler and Tchouaméni.

In a recent development, if Valverde’s extension is confirmed, none of the three midfielders would have a contract ending before 2031. That would remove contract questions over a key part of the squad for several seasons. The two completed renewals arrived during the build-up to a busy run of home matches.

According to recent reports, 🚨🤍 Aurelien Tchouameni has signed upcoming long term deal at Real Madrid until June 2032. pic.twitter.com/13BtcLyubP.

— Fabrizio Romano (@FabrizioRomano) November 19, 2026.

Tchouaméni has not been fully clear of fitness concerns this month. Earlier in November he left the France squad with a muscle problem. He was back in training with the Madrid squad on the day his renewal was announced.

In a recent development, real Madrid host Celta at the Santiago Bernabéu on Saturday 21 November at 21:00 in LaLiga matchday 13. PSV then visit for a Champions League game on Tuesday 24 November.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Former Roma and Paris Saint-Germain attacker Javier Pastore has shared his thoughts ahead of the meeting of his two former clubs in the Champions League on Wednesday evening, and has explained what makes the two teams so enjoyable to watch: ‘Gasperini has made his philosophy clear to the players, like Lucho at PSG’.
  • Roma face another tough test in the Champions League away against the reigning champions, PSG, on Wednesday night.
  • PSG, meanwhile, have had a perfect start and will be looking to make it five wins from five on Wednesday night.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former Roma and Paris Saint-Germain attacker Javier Pastore has shared his thoughts ahead of the meeting of his two former clubs in the Champions League on Wednesday evening, and has explained what makes the two teams so enjoyable to watch: ‘Gasperini has made his philosophy clear to the players, like Lucho at PSG’.

Roma face another tough test in the Champions League away against the reigning champions, PSG, on Wednesday night. The Giallorossi have four points from their opening four matches in the competition this season after tests away against Fenerbahce and Manchester United and at home against Slovan Bratislava and Real Madrid.

PSG, meanwhile, have had a perfect start and will be looking to make it five wins from five on Wednesday night. Luis Enrique’s side have beaten Slovan Bratislava, Manchester City, Barcelona and Villarreal already this season.

“Both play to impose themselves with great talents in attack,” said Pastore in an interview with La Gazzetta dello Sport. “They have coaches who work differently, but with the same attacking and counter-attacking principles. PSG will be more confident and have a perfect record, Roma need to pick up points. It will be an exciting game.”.

Pastore feels that the coaches might be both sides’ strongest assets.

“Both know how to get into their players’ heads. They are not just good tactically, but also at managing their teams, which is fundamental in modern football. I don’t know Gasperini very well, but he did great things at Atalanta and he’s brought an offensive, selfless style of play to Roma. They take risks and have lots of quality going forwards.

“He’s made his philosophy clear to the players, like Lucho at PSG, where he has changed the game concepts and the players’ mentality, who still follow him after winning two Champions Leagues.”.

Pastore pinpointed the players that Roma should be wary of.

“I’ve always liked Doue and Kvaratskhelia, who won’t be involved unfortunately, but also Mendes and Hakimi, the best full-backs in the world. I also like everything about Neves, a very special player who doesn’t always draw attention, but always helps his team in recovery, building from the back, creating space, looking for smart passes and arriving in front of goal. He’s a complete player.”.

According to recent reports, “For Roma, Dybala is a spectacle, dangerous anywhere. Malen is better than any other striker this year. And there’s also Soule, who brings something different, is technical and dribbles and scores well.”.

Alarmingly for Roma, Pastore states that there are no weaknesses in the PSG side.

It has been revealed that “I don’t see any, but maybe they will come out while the game is in progress. PSG are a united team built on the consistency of their play both in attack and defence. And Gasperini is following a similar path with Roma, always wanting to score one more than the opponent. You could even see it against Real Madrid, despite the result.”.

Still, Malen’s form is encouraging. The Dutchman has scored 16 goals from 15 games across all competitions and netted four goals during Roma’s 5-1 win over Parma on Sunday.

“With Malen in this type of form, pretty much any ball into the box ends with a goal and it’s hard to stop him. Dybala is dangerous in every situation: From free-kicks, from the edge of the area, with an assist or a shot into the top corner. These are the types of players who usually give you something extra in games like this.”.

Recent findings suggest that and lastly, when asked if he had to pick a side, Pastore mentioned: “Rome is beautiful with wonderful people, a place I lived for three great years. I’m in Paris more often because I got married there, and my children were born there. But I would take the Italian food anywhere.”.
